title: Glorious athletics campaign ends in an empty stadium near midnight
text:
The final moment of celebration in Australia's glorious athletics campaign at the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games was hilariously understated.

Approaching midnight, Lachlan Kennedy, Calab Law, Josh Azzopardi, Rohan Browning and Chris Ius finally walked onto the podium to receive their gold medals for the men's 4x100-metre relay.

The crowd had long since filed out of Scotstoun Stadium when the medal ceremony, which was supposed to happen two and a half hours earlier, kicked off.

The track and field that had hosted seven golds, five silvers and five bronze medals for Australia on a jam-packed day, had been leaf-blown, cleaned and stripped of most of its Games paraphernalia.

The stadium was empty when the medal ceremony took place. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Only a handful of volunteers, family, stadium crew, media members and team support staff remained to applaud the historic relay winners, Australia's first since 1974.

A protest by the initially disqualified Canadian team had finally succeeded, reinstating the Olympic champions to the silver medal spot and cutting short Ghanaian celebrations of bronze deep in the bowels of the Glasgow Warriors' rugby club home ground.

In a credit to organisers, the pyrotechnics still fired, the flags were still raised by military personnel in full regalia, and the anthem still played over the stadium PA.

Lachlan Kennedy, Josh Azzopardi, Calab Law, Rohan Browning and Chris Ius eventually got their moment. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Advance Australia Fair was sung even more drone-fully than usual without the safety of a crowd to hide the nasal tones of the Aussie accent, before the small gathering shuffled off the track.

It was a bizarrely low-key moment for one of the crowning achievements of this breakout meet for Team Australia, equalling the most medals won by the track and field team at a Commonwealth Games on foreign soil.

Of the 12 gold medals, 11 silver, and 11 bronzes, none sums up what the team has and can become more than this relay triumph.

Administrators, cheerleaders and athletes alike have been spruiking this new golden generation for Australian Athletics, which has pumped countless hours and very countable dollars into the nation's relays program in recent years.

Team Australia athletes pose for a photo after the women's and men's 4x100 metres relay finals on day nine of the Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium. (Getty Images: Paul Harding)

In the past four years, Commonwealth Games Australia invested $11.6 million into the Green2Gold2Great program.

That covered a wide range of athletes, with $500,000 dedicated to relays specifically.

In that time, Australia's teams have found some phenomenal success across a number of events.

In 2025, there were green and gold teams in all six events at the World Athletics Relays for the first time ever and the mixed 4x400m team won silver.

At this year's World Relays, the men's 4x400m picked up an Australian record and bronze.

Calab Law handed over to final runner Rohan Browning with Australia in first place. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

So well drilled are these teams that when it came time for the heats on the final morning of the athletics program, both the men's and women's teams could rest individual 100m medallists Kennedy and Torrie Lewis.

Azzopardi put aside his bitter disappointment at only being brought to Glasgow as a relay runner to contribute to the cause, describing the heats as "a training run".

That is a far cry from the team that missed out in Birmingham because Browning took a tumble in the heats.

They missed the 2024 Olympic final despite running faster heat times than the top three in the opposite heat, mucked up the final change in last year's world championships final, and missed a medal by just 0.24 of a second at World Relays in May.

This gold medal puts the world on notice, and there is still more room to grow.

Lachlan Kennedy, Joshua Azzopardi, Calab Law and Rohan Browning celebrate victory in the men's 4x100m relay final at Scotstoun Stadium. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

It is a credit to the system and their confidence in it that they didn't rush Glasgow 100m finalist Eddie Nketia into the team, even for the heats, opting instead for quick-start specialist Ius to lead off.

Kennedy replaced him for the final, playing his role to perfection, handing off cleanly to Azzopardi deep in the box, before Law and Browning came home in 38.07.

"We knew what we had in us, we're training well, we compete domestically all year against each other, [so] we're pretty used to each other. I think it's a big part of why we're so successful. Train together all year, camps all year," Kennedy said.

Kennedy said there is no first and second squad in their team, but 1A and 1B, described as "green and gold" by Browning, who flagged the looming arrivals of Gout Gout and Nketia once they have more time to train with the team that now carries a golden aura.

"I hope there are kids at home tonight watching this who aspire to grow up and be part of this team," Browning said.

"Not just aspire to the baggy green or the Wallabies or the Australian AFL team, aspire to be part of the Australian relay team."

We have already seen glimpses of it, with former Cronulla Sharks under-17 player Zavier Peacock opting for the track and finishing second behind Gout at this year's junior Australian titles.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

And veteran Kurtis Marschall was spurred on by their performance.

The back-to-back-to-back Commonwealth Games pole vault champion started his competition first and finished last on a frigid summer's night in Glasgow, getting the chance to watch his teammates pick up medals as he made his way up to a Games record of 5.85m, claiming the last Aussie gold of the program.

"The system is working. The boys' relay tonight was just phenomenal. They inspired me to get over the line," he said.

"We just want to keep pushing this sport along more and more and more. It's the best sport in the world and deserves more eyes, so we're just doing our part."

The whole stadium was watching his crowning moment and while no-one saw "the boys" get theirs, they weren't there to see the work it took to get there either.

title: Garma land council announcement sparks concern in region
text:
The announcement of a new remote Northern Territory land council has taken some Yolŋu leaders by surprise, with a key clan group elder initially rejecting the prospect of taking part.

Yothu Yindi Foundation chairman and Gumatj elder Djawa Yunupiŋu yesterday made the bold announcement at the Garma Festival of the plan to create the new Dilak Land Council.

"This land council is the vision of our elders who knew one day, when the time was right, the power would be brought back fully into the hands of the land owners," he said.

The announcement came on the 50th anniversary of the federal Aboriginal Land Rights Act, and would mark the first new land council to be formed in the NT in about 35 years.

If the Dilak Land Council comes to fruition, it will be a breakaway from the powerful Northern Land Council (NLC), which controls mining royalty distribution across the Top End.

Mr Yunupiŋu pledged the new council would still work in partnership with the NLC.

Djawa Yunupiŋu announced a land council to be led by the Dilak of north-east Arnhem land. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

In reaction to the announcement, an elder of another of the Gove Peninsula's leading clan groups, the Rirratjiŋu, has told the ABC he would not join the new council.

"I'm not happy and I'm not going to it," Rirratjiŋu Aboriginal Corporation chairman Wanyubi Marika said.

"I have to go back to my lawyers and find a way how to work on this. At the moment I don't agree with it, I just stick to the Rirratjiŋu current Northern Land Council program and support to Rirratjiŋu."

'Top of the mountain': New breakaway land council announced at Garma Fifty years since the creation of the Aboriginal Land Rights Act, a major shake-up of the land rights system has been announced at the Garma Festival.

The Gumatj and Rirratjiŋu clans have had a tense modern history together, and had been caught up in years-long court battles over the division of mining royalties in the region.

While those tensions have been healing in recent years, Mr Marika said he felt "frustrated and confused" by the latest move, and criticised what he said was a lack of consultation.

"This thing was thrown into my face, like an ambush," he said.

"I don't want to be surprised like that, because I never went through those discussions in the past. That kind of surprise is not accepted by me, or by the Rirratjiŋu clan.

"I will be open [to consultations], but I will not agree from Rirratjiŋu point of view.

"Because, strongly, we, in a power under the Northern Land Council, and under the Land Rights Act, we have more power, control over our land and for development and for working with our government and stakeholders … and not other clan groups that are involved."

Mr Yunupiŋu said in a further statement that Mr Marika and other Rirratjiŋu elders were consulted over the new land council prospect as were all of Gove's 13 clan groups.

"We will continue to engage with all the other clans as we progress this important work," he said.

Yiŋiya Guyula has also voiced some concerns over the new Dilak Land Council proposal. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Arnhem Land politician voices concern

Another senior Yolŋu elder and local leader, independent NT politician and Djambarrpuyŋu clan elder Yiŋiya Guyula, has also voiced some concerns over the new Dilak Land Council proposal.

"I've not been included in these current discussions of a new land council announced at Garma and neither have my clan elders," he said.

"The name Dilak is something that is worrying for me because we need to make sure that a new land council is inclusive of all Yolŋu, and the Dilak Council is a group currently associated with the Miwatj area in the eastern part of our Yolŋu country and we need to have a close look at who is included in this land council and who is creating the foundation for a very powerful new body.

"There are many clans across Yolŋu country.

"We need to create equality for all Yolŋu clans and we don't want to fall into a trap of a new land council that is not truly representative of Yolŋu rom [law]."

However, Mr Guyula also said that he would back a Yolŋu-run land council for the region.

"I am very interested to hear more," he said.

"I am supportive of a Yolŋu land council but this process needs to come under the Yolŋu system of law, led by our people, and inclusive of all our clans without balanda [non-Indigenous people] influence or control in the background."

Malarndirri McCarthy says the looming closure of a Rio Tinto mine will bring big changes to north-east Arnhem Land. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Formal process still to go through

Minister for Indigenous Australians Malarndirri McCarthy would have to sign off on a formal proposal to authorise the creation of the Dilak Land Council before it could happen.

Yesterday she said she was yet to receive such a proposal.

Ms McCarthy also acknowledged that Mr Yunupiŋu's family had been speaking about the prospect of a new land council for many years, and said the announcement was respectful.

"There was absolute respect and I think that was important too, because they know that there's still many steps to go before anything is official," she said.

The announcement of the land council comes at a precarious time for the Gove Peninsula, as the region prepares for the end of its major employer, a Rio Tinto bauxite mine, in 2029.

Also during the Garma Festival, NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro announced that an "in-principle" agreement had been made with the Rirratjiŋu clan, which would ensure the town lease of Nhulunbuy would be handed back to the Rirratjiŋu after the end of the mine.

title: Love story: We brought home three orphaned children on the same day
text:
Mark and Anna Dombkins were a young married couple, enjoying life with their six-month-old son in Wollongong/Dharawal lands, when a show documenting the horrors of an international orphanage changed the trajectory of their lives.

It compelled the pair to move overseas and adopt displaced children into their own loving and growing family.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

We had no idea what our family would become

Anna: Mark and I met at our church youth group.

He was just such a good human that I started to be like, "OK, this could be serious, he could be the one."

We did talk about wanting to have kids, we wanted to have a bigger family, which to us kind of meant maybe three or four biological children.

Loading...

Mark: When I met Anna, we were probably 16, and I just remember thinking, "she's beautiful and such a kind, endearing, warm person".

We both came from families where we had one sibling.

A mutual friend we had — there were five kids in his family — and I used to go to his place after school all the time, and it'd be a riot, it was so much fun.

I really liked the idea of a big family.

We needed to do something

Anna: Our son Jackson was six months old when we stumbled across a documentary called The Dying Rooms.

It was created by some journalists who went into orphanages in China and took a hidden camera.

We saw not just one room, but rooms and rooms full of babies who were never held and never picked up by anybody.

And there we were with this one little baby who was so loved, and there was always a line-up of people ready to hold him.

It just broke our heart.

It was just a very clear moment where we sat there thinking, "OK, we need to do something."

That's when we really just decided to grow our family in part through adoption.

Why don't we move to Africa?

Anna: We spent three years trying to adopt a child in Australia and we hadn't even been approved to start on the seven-year waiting list yet.

By that stage we were delighted to have another baby of our own, Jemima.

Mark and I were walking along the beach one day and I said to Mark, "what if we just move to Africa?"

And he just said, "yes, let's do that."

Between that conversation and landing in Tanzania was about six months, so it was a whirlwind.

Tanzania just ticked all the boxes; it was safe for us to live in with two young children, it was a place we could both work [Mark as a teacher and me as a school counsellor] and live, and we could legally adopt as Australians.

Finding the [particular] baby home was one of the things that led us to Tanzania because our big priority was finding children who were legitimately abandoned and where the processes were honourable and ethical.

Anna lived in Tanzania for three years. (Supplied)

Mark: I didn't want to get old in 20 years, look back and go, "we both felt strongly about this thing, but we just didn't have the guts to make it happen.

So, relocating to Africa, it was almost a relief that Anna would suggest it.

Reading the stories from the baby home [we found] and what the team there were aspiring to do, which was keep biological families together wherever possible, was also such a relief.

Because our intention was to do something good, but we didn't want good intentions to have bad impacts that we weren't aware of.

We brought home three of them on that one day

Anna: We'd been in Tanzania a couple of months when we got an email about a set of twins who needed a family.

The baby home had gone through the processes to try and find other ways they could be reunified with their biological family and those had all failed.

I remember just seeing Shay and Charlie in this sea of other babies. Jemima and I sat with them, and the connection was pretty immediate.

Then as we spent time with Amy, who ran the baby home, she told us that the twins actually had a brother [Jabari] who was only nine months older.

He was so malnourished, he wasn't likely to survive.

And really, she was saying, "can you take him home?"

Anna and Mark adopted twins Shay and Charlie, and their older brother Jabari. (Supplied)

So, we brought home the three of them on that one day.

We then had one four-year-old and four one-year-olds at home.

But it was just the most beautiful thing watching two sets of siblings come together and make a family.

And watching Jabari, the brother who was so unwell, come to life before our eyes with good food and love and care, was just incredible.

Baby number six was on the way

Anna: We spent three years in Tanzania before we moved back to Australia.

Max was born when the family of seven returned to live in Australia. (Supplied)

We'd been home two weeks when I started feeling really tired.

And then we discovered baby number six was on the way.

It was crazy timing, but it was something we look back on now and think we never would have planned that, but it was so perfect.

Having Max just bookended our family in a way that allowed Shay, Jabari and Charlie to also welcome another child.

It's their story now, we get to cheer them on

Mark: A big family is both exhausting and so rewarding — it is beautiful chaos.

You see through their eyes, like the innocence and just the beautiful naivety of kids where they don't see colour and they don't see all the things that the world sees.

Anna and Mark with their children, (from left) Jabari, Shay, Max, Jemima, Charlie and Jackson. (Supplied)

Just learning about their love in all the most beautiful ways just really grounds and teaches you as an adult.

And to have gone on that journey with [Anna], the person I love and my best friend … and being truly known by someone and knowing someone in that way through the highs and lows ... it's just made it even more special.

Anna: They make us better and yes, we have helped them, but really our other children are so blessed by having them in our family as well.

They have a broader perspective.

They have a deeper emotional capacity, and their world has expanded by having the family that we have.

It's a wild ride and it takes everything we have every day, but there's so much joy in it.

Anna and Mark's foundation, Forever Projects, is working to end the orphan crisis in Tanzania through income creation for women. (Supplied)

Mark and I have been each other's support through it all and we see each other's best and worst self.

And we're there for each other through it all.

We don't know what the future holds for our kids, but we just can't wait to watch.

It's their story now and we just get to cheer them on and watch.

title: After javelin gold, Aussie star heads straight back to hospital work
text:
Sydney doctor Mackenzie Little has finally become a golden girl with the javelin as she led one last parade of Commonwealth Games field event medallists in the green and gold.

The remarkable 29-year-old Little, a doctor at Northern Beaches Hospital, can barely even call herself a part-time athlete these days, such is her busy medical life, but she still proved too good for her opponents as she finally lifted a major international title.

She nailed victory with her first throw and then revealed she will be jetting straight back to work on Tuesday as an ear, nose and throat registrar.

On a night when pole vaulter Kurtis Marschall completed Australia's golden track-and-field program by soaring to a Games-record 5.85 metres and a third-straight title, Little's achievement felt even more astonishing.

"I'm so I'm relieved and excited — this is so fantastic. Nailing the first throw is maybe something to do with how my training's been a bit quality over quantity in the last couple of years," she said.

"I wish I could say, you know, that I'm really, really training my butt off, but I'm just having to fit things in around my job. I'm having to make the most of sometimes challenging situations, not having all the time in the world.

"I perform surgeries and see outpatients in clinics and take care of patients who are in the ward sick in hospital. Then in the evenings, I'll get to training, but I've had to change my training locations this year to stay within 30 minutes of the hospital. When you're on call, you need to — overnight and in the evenings — be within 30 minutes of the hospital in case of emergencies.

"I'm gonna go and fly home straight away and get back to work."

On a tricky night for throwers in the Scotstoun Stadium on the last evening of track and field competition, Little believed her technique of throwing low and hard to cut through the wind helped her to a season best 61.88m with an opener that no-one else threatened.

New Zealand silver medallist Tori Moorby hurled 60.08m in the third round to grab the silver, while Kenya's Irene Jepkemboi took the bronze.

Kurtis Marschall reacts after securing his third Commonwealth Games gold medal in the pole vault. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Marschall, winner at both the Gold Coast and Birmingham Commonwealth Games, finished the night in style by becoming only the third Australian ever to win three titles in a row in the same event, and ending with a leap that surpassed his hero Steve Hooker's 5.80m in Melbourne 20 years ago.

Entering the competition late, the hot favourite from Adelaide held his nerve to defeat South African silver medallist Kyle Rademeyer and England's bronze winner Owen Heard (both 5.70m).

It was the latest big achievement for the 29-year-old, who earlier in the season handed a once-in-a-blue-moon defeat to the sport's modern-day legend, Armand 'Mondo' Duplantis.

"I just wanted to solidify myself in the record books, like I already did with the gold medal, but I definitely wanted to jump that 5.85 and take it off Steve," Marschall said.

Brooke Buschkuehl in action and on her way to bronze in the long jump. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Melbourne's Brooke Buschkuehl, the indefatigable 33-year-old mum, also made it a hat-trick of medals, but again missed out on the one she really wanted as she added a bronze in the long jump to go with her two silvers from Gold Coast and Birmingham.

Promising Wollongong teenager Delta Amidzovski, the 19-year-old world junior long jump champion, finished fourth, just five centimetres off a podium place.

title: Victorian premier 'happy' to appear before Big Build royal commission
text:
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll says he would be "happy" to appear before a royal commission into construction sector corruption, but has rejected any immediate help from the state opposition in determining terms of reference for the inquiry.

A royal commission into corruption in Victoria's Big Build was the first thing Mr Carroll announced after he took over from Jacinta Allan as premier last week.

Opposition leader Jess Wilson has released her party's proposed terms of reference for the royal commission and said she won't support terms that are devised by Labor alone.

Ms Wilson described the opposition's proposed terms of reference as "non-negotiable."

At the top of the opposition's witness wish list was former premier Daniel Andrews, construction sector mediator Mick Gatto, disgraced former CFMEU boss John Setka and recently-resigned premier Jacinta Allan.

The opposition listed former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan as potential witnesses in their royal commission proposal. (AAP Image: Daniel Pockett)

Mr Carroll and his deputy leader Gabrielle Williams were also on the opposition's 25-person list of witnesses to be called in its proposed terms of reference.

On Sunday morning Mr Carroll said he "would be happy" to give evidence if required, but dismissed the opposition's proposed terms of reference and witness list as a "stunt".

"The opposition are about stunts, I'm about deeds not words," Mr Carroll said.

"I'm working with the chief commissioner and getting on with the job of the terms of reference for the royal commission."

Mr Carroll said he had not read the opposition's proposals for the royal commission.

"I will read it but we haven't been able to find it. I think the media got a copy of it before I did and I've asked my office to track down a copy," he said.

Last week, former commissioner of Victoria's Independent Broad-based Anti-Corruption Commission (IBAC), Robert Redlich, said Mr Andrews and Ms Allan should "undoubtedly" be called to give evidence before the royal commission.

Mr Carroll would not say whether he believed Mr Andrews and Ms Allan should be called as witnesses, as proposed by the opposition.

"Everyone should be questioned that the royal commission believes had a role," he said.

"That'll be a matter for the commissioner and the terms of reference. They'll be wide and they'll be exhaustive."

Jess Wilson says the opposition will not support terms of reference for the royal commission that are set by labor alone. (ABC News)

Ms Wilson rejected Mr Carroll's characterisation of the opposition's proposed terms of reference.

"I say to the premier, integrity is not a stunt. Victorians deserve answers, they deserve to know how their money has gone from these worksites into the pockets of criminals," she said.

"Ben Carroll sat next to Jacinta Allan for three years. He endorsed every single decision that this premier made."

In a letter to the premier accompanying the opposition's proposed terms of reference, Ms Wilson said the inquiry should extend beyond the CFMEU.

"Since the scandal first became public, further information has emerged that demonstrates the inquiry must extend beyond the conduct of one union," she wrote.

"It must examine the broader system through which major projects have been selected, procured, administered and funded.

"As you rightly identified in your press conference yesterday, those terms of reference must be expansive. They must also specifically examine — at public hearings as a matter of urgency –the knowledge and culpability of what current and former Premiers, Ministers and senior officials knew."

Ms Wilson said her party would not support "narrow terms designed by Labor alone" or the appointment of a commissioner without consultation.

title: Australia records biggest-ever surge in EV sales
text:
Australia has recorded its biggest-ever quarterly surge in electric vehicle sales, with updated figures showing new EV purchases doubled in the three months to June 30.

At 49 per cent, nearly one in every two new vehicles sold was either electric or hybrid, with the spike coinciding with soaring fuel prices at the start of April following the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz at the end of February.

The data from the Australian Automobile Association shows that the fully electric vehicle market share jumped from 12.25 per cent to more than 21 per cent in six months.

(Supplied: AAA)

It means fully electric vehicles outperformed hybrid model EVs for the first time, despite hybrids recording their second-highest share on record.

Meanwhile, the market share of non-electric vehicle sales took a nosedive, falling to 50.84 per cent of June quarter sales, down from 64.23 per cent.

Liberal deputy leader Jane Hume says the figures show government subsidies are not needed. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Opposition says EV subsidies 'out of control'

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume told Insiders the figures showed the electric vehicle market does not need more government subsidies, which she said had "run out of control".

EV tax discount removed two days' worth of carbon emissions Two days' worth of carbon emissions were removed thanks to the $2 billion electric vehicle tax discount. But its supporters say that put 64,000 more EVs on the road, jump-starting the struggling industry.

"I think that's the market speaking with its feet, and probably why we don't necessarily need more subsidies on electric vehicles," she said.

"Unfortunately, the subsidy program that's been run by this government has run out of control, and it's costing Australians more and more."

In May's federal budget, the government announced a slow winding down of its generous tax discounts that encouraged more people to buy EVs, which will save $1.7 billion over four years.

The discount was introduced to consumers at the start of 2023 and made electric vehicles thousands of dollars cheaper through an exemption to fringe benefit tax.

The scheme has been adopted at a rate far beyond the government's expectations and, as of May, was expected to cost $1.35 billion this year alone, well above the initial forecast of $90 million.

Discount to roll back from April

From April next year, the tax exemption will still apply to electric vehicles costing less than $75,000, but those above that threshold will only get a 25 per cent discount on the fringe benefits tax.

Warning laws lacking for new car market As an influx of car brands enters the market, dealers ask for a change to consumer laws to fix a grey area that makes them responsible for warranty repairs.

From April 2029, all electric vehicles below the luxury car tax threshold will receive a 25 per cent tax discount.

Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen has previously said the government was scrapping the discount because it had done its job, creating a boom in EV uptake that has driven investment in charging stations and other infrastructure.

With more Australians driving EVs, car dealers are now calling on the federal government to update Australian Consumer Law to better protect Australians who purchase EVs from manufacturers overseas.

title: Historic strike, YouTuber's fate features in photo picks for June, July
text:
Welcome to our extended photo wrap for June and July, taking a look at eight weeks of news coverage from our photographers.

June

Bird flu arrives in Australia

Toni Howlett said avian influenza had not crossed her mind when she found the bird. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

It was a chance encounter on an Esperance beach in mid-June that led to the discovery of Australia's first H5 bird flu case.

Dr Toni Howlett found the migratory brown skua bird, which was later confirmed as H5 positive.

The disease has been detected across several states since then, with authorities and farmers watching closely.

Socceroo kids

Students celebrate watching the game, which ended in a draw. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

While some older viewers were at the pub for the 10am start time for the World Cup match between Australia and Paraguay in late June, students at Lynwood Senior High School were watching eagerly from the classroom.

The school has run its own soccer academy for the past two decades, and students had put together their own version of the World Cup, playing matches during lunchtime on Thursday.

Worst storm in 49 years

A crew spent the morning removing the weight of the tree from the house before covering the hole in the roof. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

As the clock ticked over to the first minutes of June, a substantial storm was battering Perth and parts of southern WA.

Emergency services received more than 800 calls for help, including from residents in Greenwood, where a tree fell on a house.

Albany shark attack

The 35-year-old diver was taken by boat to shore but could not be revived. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

It's been a devastating few months for some in the spearfishing community, with two shark attack deaths in WA making global headlines.

This was the scene from the emergency response to the death of 35-year-old Daniel Turpin, who had been diving near Albany.

Hanson in Perth

Pauline Hanson hit the road to campaign in the west. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Riding a wave of popularity in the polls, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson made a visit to Perth to meet supporters in mid-June.

During the trip, she revealed she took policy advice from Australia's richest person, Gina Rinehart, and was planning for her party to contest Labor seats in WA's 2029 election.

Reconciliation

Elders say the Welcome to Country connects people to their country and culture, and to each other. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

During Reconciliation Week, which ended in early June, Aboriginal elders explained the importance of Welcome to Country ceremonies, which were met by racist heckling on Anzac Day.

For some elders, the practice is about connection and preserving history.

A ceremony is seen here in front of the statue of 19th-century Whadjuk elder Balbuk Yooreel at the Government House Gardens.

Turtle homecoming

The loggerhead turtles have been cared for in Bunbury for two years. (ABC News: Renee Hilton Jones )

In some good news, two loggerhead turtles cared for in Bunbury have been rehabilitated and were set to be released into the wild, embarking on a 1,400 kilometre journey to Ningaloo Reef.

There were tears and cheers when volunteers and staff said their farewells to the turtles, Squirdle and Treasure.

July

Labor stalwart resigns

Paul Papalia and Roger Cook share a hug, marking the end of almost 20 years in parliament. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

The first week of July marked the end of senior WA minister Paul Papalia's almost two-decade political career.

Mr Papalia held portfolios including corrective services, defence industries, emergency services and veterans affairs, and made the announcement alongside Premier Roger Cook.

The resignation triggered a by-election in Mr Papalia's electorate of Secret Harbour.

Yung Filly in court

The trial of Yung Filly spanned almost two weeks, reaching a conclusion on Friday. (ABC News: David Weber )

On the last day of July, a decision was made in the trial of UK YouTuber and rapper Yung Filly.

A jury found the entertainer, whose real name is Andres Barrientos, not guilty of raping a woman after a concert in 2024.

Three further counts of rape were undecided, and he was found guilty of assaulting the 20-year-old woman.

BHP strike

More than 100 workers stopped work at BHP's Port Hedland operations for an eight-hour strike. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

In WA's north, BHP workers in Port Hedland downed tools, in one of the most significant industrial disputes in a quarter of a century.

More than 100 workers walked off the job at Australia's busiest port, and were met with sausage sizzles and supporters.

Wave Rock wall

The wall was built in 1928 and helps divert water into the Wave Rock Reservoir. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

ABC Great Southern's Astrid Volzke offered a different angle to the well-known Wave Rock tourist attraction, focusing on an almost 100-year-old wall at the site.

The wall, crumbling in places, has sparked conversation among locals about whether it should be preserved or removed.

Flower clones

The first Queen of Sheba orchid to flower from a cloning program at Kings Park. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

The Queen of Sheba orchid, native to WA, is one of the rarest in the world with only 30 left in the wild.

But there is hope for the critically endangered flower's future, as scientists from Kings Park have successfully cloned the plant.

Idle oil rig

The Cliff Head platform has operated since 2006, but today it sits abandoned off the Dongara coastline. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

An abandoned offshore oil drilling rig in WA's Midwest is leading fishermen and conservation groups to demand the federal take action over the Cliff Head oil platform.

The company that owned it went into administration, and fishermen are worried the platform could put crayfishing grounds at risk.

title: Home owners worry about proposed 40m telco tower going up next door
text:
Property owners in a small West Australian town say they are angry and disappointed to have been kept in the dark about plans for a 40-metre-high telecommunications tower to be built adjacent to homes.

The pole and associated infrastructure will be built by NBN Co on a parcel of land on the outskirts of the Wyndham town site in WA's most northern community.

Harry Ciccotosto, who has lived near the proposed site for 15 years, is not happy about the development.

"Who's going to purchase a property where the tower is that high that if it fell over it'd knock your house down?" he said.

"It's ridiculous."

Residents say the views they enjoy across to the Cockburn Ranges will be interrupted by the tower. (Supplied: Glen Highett)

The bush block was excised from a reserve by the Shire of Wyndham East Kimberley at a council meeting in June 2025, specifically for an NBN tower and antennas.

Residents whose properties back onto the reserve said they were not officially told of the development until the shire sent out letters about the proposed tower being open to public comment from July 9 until July 30.

Property owners say notices about the development only arrived in the mail in mid-July. (Supplied: Glen Highett)

NBN Co's site selection report was only made publicly available once the consultation period had begun.

Eight sites were proposed in the report.

Neighbour of seven years Glen Highett is dismayed residents were overlooked in the site-selection process.

"There's closer proximity to residents here than the other sites," he said.

" It should never have been on the table. "

NBN Co said in a statement the Durack Road site was identified through "collaboration and consultation with the Shire and involved detailed technical, engineering, and planning assessments".

"The location was selected following feedback from the council on the suitability of the site," the statement said.

However, Mr Ciccotosto disagrees.

"Had the criteria they used to dismiss these other blocks been used on this block, it would have been the first block to be dismissed as a location because it's the closest to residents," he said.

Wyndham is Western Australia's northernmost community. (Supplied: Cambridge Gulf Limited)

Minutes from the June 2025 council meeting show "community engagement was not required" and the excision was passed unanimously.

"Not one question was asked on behalf of the ratepayers at all, it sailed through, and it's too late now," Mr Ciccotosto said.

He said while there had been no consultation or information provided to landowners by the shire or NBN until this month, works had started on the site back in January.

Wyndham is home to about 1,000 people. (ABC Kimberley: Sam Tomlin)

Mr Highett and Mr Ciccotosto are concerned about the tower's impact on their views across the Cockburn Ranges, potential health effects, and how the tower's proximity would impact on property values.

"We're feeling sick to the stomach," Mr Highett said.

NBN Co said it encouraged feedback during the public comment period.

It said the investment was to improve access to high-speed broadband connectivity for Wyndham.

The Shire of Wyndham East Kimberley did not respond to the ABC's questions about the site selected for the tower.NBN Co will build the pole and associated infrastructure;

title: Darwin live music scene keen for change as touring acts snub the Top End
text:
For local musicians like Leisa Howlett, the chance to support major touring artists playing gigs in Darwin can be game-changing.

This year Howlett's punk trio TANG played Darwin's Bass in the Grass Festival alongside punk rock royalty The Living End and a host of other acts from Australia and overseas.

"That was fantastic just to be able to say, 'Hey, we're a local Darwin act, this is what we're doing,' and build those connections," she said.

Howlett is part of a local live music ecosystem that she says is bursting with up-and-coming talent.

TANG's Leisa Howlett says Darwin's thriving local music scene is missing out on visits from touring artists. (ABC News: Mike Donelly)

But opportunities to get on stage or the road with touring acts from interstate or overseas are few and far between.

"[In the past] I've heard stories of really big bands coming and playing in venues like the [Darwin] Amphitheatre for example," she said.

"I just don't think that’s happening now."

Mark Smith, executive director of MusicNT, agrees the heyday still remembered by many Darwin music lovers has given way to a touring live performance drought.

Australian live music 'firmly in crisis' From Perth to Albury, we take a look at Australia's live music scene and how it's faring after a pandemic and during a cost of living crisis.

"There was a period where we had these huge artists coming through Darwin – I remember Stevie Wonder, Cliff Richard, Dire Straits," he said.

"That hasn't happened in recent years.

"There's a few factors there – that was [back in the day when] planes had to stop over in Darwin to refuel – but I think mainly [the reason is that] the general costs have increased."

Crowd-sourced data from the Australian Concert Tour Database shows the territory hosts a disproportionately low number of international touring artists compared to other states and territories.

With industry stakeholders saying visits from both internationally and nationally renowned artists becoming increasingly rare, they’re concerned the issue could worsen with time.

'No profitable tours' in Darwin

Live performance venues have struggled across the country in the cost-of-living crisis and since the COVID pandemic.

But in a place where airfares and accommodation costs were already high, venue managers say they are now almost guaranteed to lose money booking touring artists in the Top End capital.

Russell Temple, general manager of Darwin venue Mayberry, has been booking bands for 30 years and says he's seen the capacity to sell tickets in Darwin tank over that time.

"I'm not aware of any live music tours being profitable in Darwin," he said.

Mayberry general manager Russell Temple says most venue owners lose money when booking touring artists in Darwin. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

He said the large amount of money spent on overhead costs – often at the expense of low ticket prices – is compounded by small and historically stagnant population.

"I've been part of national tours where every other state [beside the territory] has sold their quota," he said.

"Pete Murray is one – we did shows in Alice Springs and Port Lincoln and sold over 900 in both locations [while] in Darwin we sold 240."

Ms Howlett says, in her experience, lesser-known Australian acts often rule out travelling through the territory entirely on account of the high costs and associated risks.

While live venues across the country have struggled in the cost-of-living crisis, touring costs in Darwin were already prohibitive. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"There are long distances to cover by road, there's risks with travel, and with [the cost of] insurance it's pretty daunting to plan a big tour without some funding behind you,” she said.

For Mr Temple, the lack of touring artists and the low chance of profitability run the risk of Darwin's live music woes becoming self-fulfilling.

"You don't get the industry talking in a positive manner about Darwin," he said.

Industry urges ground-up approach

Those at the heart of the local live music scene say there's a road to revival, but it will require stakeholders to think outside the box.

Mr Smith says the groundwork must be done to establish a self-sustaining local scene before bigger acts choose to take a risk visiting the Top End.

Music NT's Mark Smith wants to see a renewed focus on supporting local live music and performance venues. (ABC News: Simon Goodes)

"It's a question of 'How do we get people back out and supporting live music? What spaces do we have for bands to play in?'" he said.

"There’s a lot of discussion around redeveloping the [Darwin] Amphitheatre to bring it up to a standard where artists can use it.

"That's really a live conversation between local government and territory government."

In remote Australia, a concert becomes something much bigger Behind the scenes of the Guts tour: a roaming, solar-powered tour that snakes its way through some of the most remote communities in the Northern Territory.

He says some bigger-picture solutions would require government to work with the local scene to embolden promoters and venues to take risks.

"I think there's opportunities, almost to repurpose the existing funding structures to try and take away some of the risk for promoters to bring larger scale acts," he said.

For Ms Howlett and bands like TANG, it's a matter of tapping into the reservoirs of local talent.

"Propping up our local bands, especially at festivals like Darwin Festival and Bass in the Grass, is really important — giving local acts that chance to get on those bigger stages and build confidence," she said.

“People are hungry for it, and it's really exciting to get those opportunities and to meet these bands from other cities around Australia and show off the talent that we have here."

title: Quick hits: Sprinter's surprise, a bored prince and a stunning upset
text:
An Australian sprinter receives a surprise visit, Jamaica celebrates in style after beating the Diamonds and Prince George looks bored at the cycling.

Here are the quick hits from day nine of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Surprise guests shock Aussie sprinter

Chloe Mannix-Power (right) had some fans she was not expecting to see in the stands. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Chloe Mannix-Power somewhat controversially missed out on an individual 100-metre berth at these Games, but hit the track for the first time in the women's 4x100m heats.

In the moments after she and teammates Ebony Lane, Monique Hanlon and Georgia Harris made it through to the women's 4x100m final, Mannix-Power looked up into the stands and received quite a shock.

"I thought [my parents] were at home watching on the lounge, but no they're up in the top of the grandstand cheering me on," she said.

"My parents love a surprise moment, they've done it before, so to be honest I kind of had a little feeling they would be up there, but they never tell me they're here until the end of the race."

Mannix-Power later helped Australia finish fourth in the final.

2. Prince George bored?

Prince William, Princess Catherine and their three children took in a few of the sports on day nine.

Prince George, however, seemed as though he wanted to be anywhere else when they visited the velodrome.

Prince George watches on at the velodrome. (AP: Andrew Milligan)

Earlier, the royals watched on as the Diamonds lost 46-45 to Jamaica in a major upset in the netball semifinals.

The Prince and Princess of Wales took to Instagram to thank the athletes for putting on a show.

The Prince and Princess of Wales and their family watching the netball at the Hydro in Glasgow. (Getty Images)

"Incredible atmosphere at the Commonwealth Games today," a post from their official Instagram account read.

"Watching world-class talent compete and seeing the power of sport to bring people together is truly special.

"Thank you to everyone involved for such a wonderful day."

3. 'Absolute scenes'

Jamaica celebrates its win over the Diamonds. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Not only did the Royals take in Jamaica's shock victory, but they also witnessed some of the wildest celebrations seen at the Commonwealth Games.

After Sophie Dwyer missed the shot that would have sent the semifinal to extra time, the entire Jamaican squad celebrated like they never had before.

We lost count of how many social media videos featured the caption: "Absolute scenes."

Loading Instagram content

For the Jamaicans, this was personal.

They were still hurting from their loss to the Diamonds in the 2022 Commonwealth Games final in Birmingham.

"We're carrying a bit of vengeance from the last Commonwealth Games," Jamaica captain Shamera Sterling-Humphrey said.

"We've graduated from bronze medals. We didn't want bronze this year."

Jamaica faces New Zealand in the final, while the Diamonds meet England in the bronze medal play-off.

4. Montag admits to being 'selfish'

Elizabeth McMillen led Jemima Montag for most of the race, but did not win gold. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

It was an Australian sweep of the medals in the women's 10,000m race walk, but the fight for the gold medal between teammates was a fierce one.

Australian Elizabeth McMillen and Jemima Montag broke clear from the pack early and led for the entire race.

McMillen was at the front, with Montag her shadow just behind.

Montag's strategy was to use McMillen as protection from the wind, a tactic which worked to perfection.

McMillen's lead for the better part of 23 laps of the 25-lap race, before Montag ducked out from behind her and put on the burners in a decisive attack to claim gold.

It was a move she had no regrets over.

"In a race you have to be selfish. Unfortunately it's an individual sport, not a team," Montag said.

"If it was cycling or something with drafting, where you do change the lead around then absolutely.

"But as much as I would love to, sometimes you have to forget it's a teammate that you care about and just remember it's another competitor and it's another body that in front of you and to ultimately be selfish."

McMillen was not particularly happy, but understood.

"What can you do? That's racing for you," McMillen said.

"I did look back a few times thinking, 'Are you going to help out here?', but no. I was the rabbit today, so what are you going to do?"

5. Indian boxer explains celebration

Arundhati Choudhary celebrates in her unique way. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

India boxer Arundhati Choudhary is a beacon of positivity inside and outside the ring.

Choudhary, who won gold in the women's 70-kilogram category in Glasgow, takes inspiration from a Hindu deity, Lord Rama.

This is why she opts for a bow and arrow celebration.

"In India we have Lord Rama, who killed negativity with his bow," Choudhary explained.

"Last year I was suffering from surgery and my family was also suffering from many problems.

"So I just throw the bow and arrow and shoot all the negativity out."

title: 'Pattern of missteps': Football bodies launch stunning Infantino rebuke
text:
Successfully stopping Gianni Infantino's FIFA plan to sell World Cup profits to private investors was the first half of a high-stakes game in global soccer politics.

The second half kicked off overnight with what seemed a clear aim of ending Infantino's decade-long presidency.

"No option should be off the table," said European soccer body UEFA, whose president Aleksander Čeferin has led the fight against Infantino in a seismic week for FIFA.

"The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family."

Aleksander Čeferin (left) has been a vocal critic of Gianni Infantino's latest quest to privatise part of FIFA. (Getty Images: Nicolò Campo/LightRocket)

After that comment, the governing body for North and Central American and Caribbean soccer (CONCACAF) called for accountability, saying: "A [World Cup] proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident. It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first. This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A full review of this leadership must now take place."

Mr Infantino had proposed creating a $US20 billion ($28.5 billion) company to run the World Cup with private investors but drew backlash that grew every day since Tuesday's announcement.

The FIFA president was forced to scrap the plan early Saturday after his senior adviser who sat on a White House panel resigned and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), joined Europe and North America in opposing it.

UEFA's blistering statement

UEFA, the governing body of European soccer, issued its blistering statement hours after FIFA announced it was withdrawing its private equity plan.

"We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast-track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game," UEFA said.

"We must identify those responsible and hold them to account.

"It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, UEFA will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again."

Lise Klaveness (right) looks on as Gianni Infantino takes a selfie with a fan during the World Cup. (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

Norwegian soccer federation president Lise Klaveness, an elected member of the UEFA executive committee, said steps must be taken to protect the integrity of the sport.

"The entire framework of international football cooperation was unnecessarily put at risk in pursuit of individual interests rather than the best interests of the game," Mr Klaveness said.

"This has been visible to many for a long time, including those of us elected to positions intended to safeguard checks and balances and provide ongoing oversight. We have to recognise that these mechanisms have not worked well enough."

Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa (right) also criticised the way the privatisation plan had been rolled out. (Getty Images: Kevin C. Cox)

The president of the AFC, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, said, "The future of global football must always be shaped through proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established governance structures of our game."

Mr Infantino's audacious bid fell apart after UEFA's 55-member nations agreed Thursday to boycott the World Cup and all other FIFA competitions. CONCACAF and the AFC also said they opposed the plan.

CONCACAF's statement added that FIFA leaders have "a duty of service over power. Where that duty is not upheld, accountability cannot be optional".

FIFA's internal revolt

There was also an internal revolt.

Mr Infantino's senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned and urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.

Hours later, FIFA chief operating officer Kevin Lamour issued a statement to the Associated Press, saying FIFA staff were deceived by Infantino's lack of openness in planning the sale over recent months and that the project must not continue.

Kevin Lamour says the FIFA plan is a project of "one person". (Getty Images: Joosep Martinson)

"It is the project of one person," wrote Mr Lamour, a longtime colleague of Mr Infantino at both FIFA and UEFA.

"Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."

Mr Infantino had proposed spinning off FIFA's commercial businesses — including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women — into a $US20 billion subsidiary with 20 per cent owned by private investors.

The "anchor investor", described by FIFA, is a New York-based investment firm launched by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

This is not Infantino's first big plan to flop

A tumultuous week in international soccer is at least the third time Mr Infantino has rocked it with an ambitious plan many in the sport saw as reckless.

But the fallout from FIFA's Joshua Kushner-backed plan is the first time UEFA has acted quickly to create momentum for removing the man who was its former long-time employee.

In 2018, Mr Infantino pushed a secretive offer of $US25 billion from Japan's SoftBank to create new competitions, which posed a long-term risk to continental events for clubs and national teams.

Vladimir Putin awarded an Order of Friendship to Gianni Infantino after the 2018 World Cup in Russia. (Getty Images: Mikhail Metzel/TASS)

In 2021, Mr Infantino proposed playing World Cups every two years instead of four — an idea that also angered the International Olympic Committee where he is an elected member.

Both plans created big rifts in the sport and were eventually dropped by FIFA.

Despite the turmoil, Mr Infantino was re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.

The third time is shaping up to be different.

November 18 is the deadline for candidates to enter the next presidential contest, exactly four months ahead of the vote in Rabat, Morocco, where FIFA has its African headquarters.

FIFA statutes allow Mr Infantino one more four-year term in office. The failed spin-off venture seemed like a way to create a commissioner-like role for Mr Infantino beyond 2031, likely paying much more than his current annual salary and a bonus deal of more than $US6 million.

Gianni Infantino with Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani and Jordan's Crown Prince Hussein at the FIFA Arab Cup 2025. (Getty Images: Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto)

It would take 106 votes to ensure a majority in a contested election. Continents surely do not vote uniformly en bloc, but most of Europe's 55, plus Asia's 46 and CONCACAF's 35 FIFA members would be a solid base.

The Qatar FA issued a statement in support of Infantino on Saturday.

Its president, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa bin Ahmed Al Thani, said: "We welcome FIFA President Gianni Infantino's decision to withdraw the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal in the interest of the global football community.

"While the proposal had merit, we applaud the wisdom behind prioritising unity among Member Associations. The Qatar Football Association fully supports president Infantino's efforts to continue growing and strengthening the game globally."

title: One final clean sweep proves Aussie track stars are the real deal
text:
The main event for most of the crowd at Scotstoun Stadium lived up to the hype.

Scottish world record holder Josh Kerr utterly bossed a chaotic men's mile final, teaching Australian hope Cameron Myers a lesson in competition racing.

Twenty-year-old Myers came into the Games in phenomenal form and pledged to not let the hometown favourite out of his sight in the final, but once he was boxed in and Kerr got a break, it was curtains with half a lap to go.

Josh Kerr lit up Scotstoun. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

"He smashed me," a visibly disappointed Myers said.

The inexperienced young gun pledged to learn from it and clearly enjoyed his time in the "electric" atmosphere.

But the finale for a historic athletics program for Australia came about half an hour later, when three Australian stars lined up in the women's mile.

We're used to see it in the swimming, but this time it was an international track meet that staged a replay of the Australian championships as Abbey Caldwell, Jess Hull and Claudia Hollingsworth went around the track four times.

Stunning day of Comm Games success for Australia Australia stuns the field to claim gold in the men's 4x100m relay for the first time since 1974 on a packed night final night of athletics action.

When they ran the equivalent 1,500 metres at the national championships in April, it was a debacle.

Hollingsworth tripped Hull, which held up Caldwell, who was pipped by Sarah Billings.

Hull and Caldwell lodged protests, Hollingsworth was disqualified, and Billings was installed as national champion.

After her unusual elevation to the crown, Billings chose to only race the 800m in Glasgow, winning bronze, and her competitors from that night in Sydney stepped in as the clear fastest milers in the country.

The women pulled off the triumph Camweon Myers (right) could not. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

Lining up in the Commonwealth Games final right next to Hull, Caldwell burst off the line, while Hull held back and watched as Hollingsworth settled into the pack ahead of her.

Like the nats, it was a slow race, raising the risk of another late calamity.

Instead, with 200 metres to go, Caldwell burst clear and Hull joined her.

Hull couldn't match Caldwell but, just like when she won silver behind Rose Davies in the 5,000m, she was beaming as her teammate crossed the line ahead of her.

Abbey Caldwell crossed ahead of Jess Hull, the woman who paved the path for her. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Meanwhile, the in-stadium announcer broke the news that the podium sweep was on as Hollingsworth, seemingly boxed in with the typically rambunctious peloton, found the space and energy to burst past Naomi Korir and claim bronze.

Caldwell had predicted a podium sweep before the athletics program started in a manner portraying matter-of-fact confidence, rather than arrogant bluster.

Even after the prediction came true, it was the importance of their presence on the start line, 9.34 metres behind the spot where Caldwell snared gold 4 minutes and 39.31 seconds later, that Hull remarked upon.

"The Aussies are a force; on that start line we're a threat," she said.

"We've done it at Commonwealth level and the next step is to do it at [world] championships, get three of us in the final and then the odds are pretty high that you're gonna bring home a couple of medals."

The women's middle distance has been the jewel in the Australian track crown before the sprinters joined the party in the past couple of years.

But this podium sweep in the first female Commonwealth mile in history, Caldwell said, truly "put [them] on the map".

"We are the best and I think we can prove that we are the best and we will come and compete for those [Olympic and world] medals," she said.

"We do all wanna keep competing and we are worldwide competitors.

"Jess paved that path for us; we're here to compete internationally, we've accomplished the Commonwealth and now we move onto the big world stage."

If Glasgow 2026 was the coming-out party for Australia's new short-track guns, it marked the coming of age for Caldwell, Hull, Hollingsworth and Billings, who were holding up the tartan long before it was cool.

title: Denzel was the first in his family to go to university, but there’s a worrying drop-off in students like him
text:

NationalVictoriaEducation Denzel was the first in his family to go to university, but there’s a worrying drop-off in students like him Jackson Graham August 2, 2026 — 1:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Denzel James is less likely to be at university than most of his peers. The Yankunytjatjara man, from a remote area of South Australia, received an ATAR of 27 and is from a low-income family. Victoria University students Athraa Yousif (left), Denzel James and Brooke Theodoridis have studied under the university’s block model, which allows students to do a single subject at a time. Jason South But he is the first of his eight siblings to pursue a degree and hopes it will pave the way for them to see university as an achievable pathway as well. “I’m proud to be the first to study at uni, because I could push my two younger siblings to eventually start preparing to see whether they want to go to university too,” the first-year law student at Victoria University said.

Advertisement

The decline in the proportion of students like James across Victorian universities has been sharp. Students from low socioeconomic backgrounds made up 12.2 per cent of all undergraduate places in 2024, a drop from 15.3 per cent in 2018, the most recent federal data compiled by the Australian Centre for Student Equity and Success (ACSES) shows. While some of that is due to a 2021 change in how the data is collected, experts say the rising cost of living, greater availability of jobs and increased course fees have disproportionately affected students from disadvantaged backgrounds. “Low-socioeconomic students are, broadly speaking, going to be last on and first off across the sectors,” ACSES trials and evaluation program director Tim Pitman said.

Advertisement

“As places expand, they are taken up by the [high-socioeconomic-status] students before the low-SES students come on. And as the sector declines, the low SES students tend to go backwards.” Victoria’s big four universities – the University of Melbourne, Monash, RMIT and Deakin – had the lowest share of undergraduates from low socioeconomic backgrounds in 2024. The University of Melbourne had the lowest share of undergraduates from low socioeconomic backgrounds. Wayne Taylor The University of Melbourne, which fared worst, said that since 2023 it had prioritised programs that supported equity students, and it had seen yearly lifts in students gaining access. A Deakin University spokesperson said it was aware of a modest decline in students from low-socioeconomic backgrounds due to cost-of-living pressures, declining ATAR completion indicating different career choices, and changing patterns of demand.

Advertisement

“We watch these numbers closely and measure ourselves against them,” the spokesperson said. RMIT University has been simplifying admissions processes, and improving pathways from vocational education into university and through equity scholarships to remove barriers to entry, a spokesperson said. Victoria University vice chancellor Adam Shoemaker with Brooke Theodoridis, Denzel James and Athraa Yousif. Jason South This year, enrolments of low-socioeconomic-background students have increased at RMIT by 3 per cent for higher education and by 6 per cent for vocational education compared with the year prior. Victoria University introduced a new block model in 2017 to allow students to do a single subject at a time over four weeks – freeing up time for them to work or care for family members while studying.

Advertisement

It has correlated with completion rates among equity students increasing to 90.82 per cent in 2024, up from 82.75 per cent in 2018, the ACSES data shows. “People weren’t succeeding fast enough, well enough, strongly enough from various backgrounds,” Victoria University vice chancellor Adam Shoemaker said of why the university changed its model. “The beauty about the block model is you can work full-time if you’re lucky enough to have a paid job and study full-time. It’s just one subject at a time.” Since the introduction of the model, fail grades for low-socioeconomic students in STEM subjects have dropped by 46.4 per cent. High distinctions have increased by 82.3 per cent for equity students, and distinctions by 52.5 per cent. “The quality has been exactly the same. The dimensions of the assessment haven’t been weakened, it’s just the performance has gotten better from students,” Shoemaker said.

Advertisement

Denzel James said the block program had helped him divide his time and achieve better outcomes. Related Article University University of Melbourne toppled from top spot in global rankings “I can give my full attention to it, not trying to balance different classes and assessments and assignments. I get that opportunity to understand the content more deeply and produce better quality work,” he said. Recent psychology graduate Athraa Yousif was also the first in her family to go to university, after moving to Australia as a refugee from Iraq. She had studied education at another university but found the large cohort overwhelming while also having caring responsibilities for her family.

When she started university, she was initially still developing her English and the model’s small class sizes suited her. “There were a lot of educational gaps as well throughout that refugee journey. title: ‘Olympic-level singing’: London’s legendary Proms offer low-cost thrills in troubled times
text:
Advertisement

WorldEuropeLondon ‘Olympic-level singing’: London’s legendary Proms offer low-cost thrills in troubled times David Crowe August 2, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: There’s a buzz in the warm evening air as thousands of people stream onto the streets near Hyde Park and talk happily about the concert they’ve just seen at a London landmark. We are outside the Royal Albert Hall a little after 9pm, a few minutes after sunset, and the cloudless sky is cornflower blue. I weave through the crowd to find some choir members who have just finished performing. This is the BBC Proms, one of the world’s great music festivals, and tonight’s concert was just one of 86 that will attract thousands this summer. “When the Proms season comes, life changes; a kind of light comes into your diary,” the BBC’s David Attenborough once said. I can see why his remark is quoted so often: it captures the audience’s sheer enthusiasm for weeks of great music. Last Night of The Proms: A quintessentially British experience. AP Over the past weeks and months, I’ve been spending time on some of the unhappy aspects of British life. I’ve met the marginalised people of Luton, the frustrated voters of Wigan and the angry protesters of London who want to stop migration. It was time to enjoy some of the things that can make London life so wonderful. I’ve just emerged from a concert where the Sydney Philharmonia Choirs joined the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra and its Chorus in a performance of Harmonium by John Adams. This was another Australian coup –the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra performed here last year – reflecting how orchestras and choirs from around the world want to be at the Proms.

Advertisement

By the time the audience sings at the Last Night of the Proms on September 12, this year’s festival will probably have reached an audience of 300,000 in person, in addition to several million viewers online and, on the famed last night, a television audience of 3.7 million. This British tradition is still going strong. Setting for the Proms, London’s landmark Royal Albert Hall. David Levene The first choir member I find is Joel Wilkinson, 24, a music teacher from Sydney. He’s on a high after the performance because he has seen the Proms online but has never made it to England. “To get to be in that room and actually perform is ... a pretty surreal experience,” he says. Teresa Benton, 61, is a software developer who joined the Sydney choir only last year after moving from Melbourne. Raised in Glen Waverley, she sang for 36 years with the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra Chorus and its predecessor, the Melbourne Chorale. “To be in the Royal Albert Hall is just something so special,” she tells me. It took months of preparation and practice. Sisters Emily and Lily Harris say the work was intense. “We had about a month of rehearsals before the flight over, and quite intensive rehearsals,” says Emily, a student at the Sydney Conservatorium of Music. In Birmingham, before they got to the Proms, they rehearsed once or twice daily. “It was a lot – almost six hours sometimes,” says Lily, a digital video director.

Advertisement

Will they get to enjoy London in summer? Not much. The choir has more performances coming up, so there is little time to relax. “I think we’ve got two brunches,” jokes Lily. But the sisters can claim a rare family achievement: their grandmother, Sue, sang at the Proms as a member of the Sydney Philharmonia Choirs; their father, Mark, performed there with the Australian Youth Orchestra. Who else in Australia can claim three generations at the Proms? Related Article Analysis

Immigration How the storming of Ceuta shifts Europe to the right As athletes are representing Australia at the Commonwealth Games, it seems appropriate for musicians to be doing the same at the Proms. Brett Weymark, the artistic director of the Sydney Philharmonia Choirs, says it’s a fair comparison because the music festival attracts performers from around the world. “It’s incredibly special that we’re here this time because it has been the better part of 16 years since we were last here,” he says. And he calls the work tonight, Harmonium, one of the most exacting pieces a chorus can perform. “This is Olympic-level choral singing,” he says. “What the athletes are doing in Glasgow, we’re doing here.” Political life in Britain is riven with anxiety about the nation’s economic and social problems, and it is not hard to see the divide between rich and poor. Life in London is easy for those with a club in St James’s and a house in the country, but it can be crushingly hard for the working poor who get by on a minimum wage of £12.71 per hour. (That’s about $24, which is $2 less than the Australian minimum wage.) Going out can be a luxury.

Advertisement

It does not have to be too expensive at the Proms, however. Every morning, people can buy £8 tickets online for the arena and gallery at the Royal Albert Hall. This is standing room only for the “Prommers” – the dedicated audience members who stamp their feet when happy and yell out “Heave” and “Ho” whenever a piano is wheeled on stage. More of that British tradition. Related Article Entertainment Why video game music is the future of orchestral concerts Call me old-fashioned, or simply lazy, but I chose a comfortable seat instead, and I got even more comfortable after a G&T. The Prommers, in their shorts and joggers, or their summer frocks, seemed to be having more fun than the couple in the royal box. (No, not members of the royal family – just people with connections.) Even in these hard times, then, it is still possible to enjoy something that is quintessentially British, on a beautiful summer night, for the cost of a bus fare and an £8 ticket. You can’t see a Premier League match for that, nor a day of Test cricket at Lord’s. No wonder everyone sings Land of Hope and Glory on the last night of the Proms.
