title: Resign or we’ll vote to oust you: Europe’s threat to Infantino
text:
Advertisement

SportSoccerFIFA World Cup Resign or we’ll vote to oust you: Europe’s threat to Infantino Tom Morgan August 2, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Gianni Infantino is facing an ultimatum from European football’s governing body UEFA: resign or face an emergency no-confidence vote. It is understood all 55 of UEFA’s member nations would opt to oust Infantino in a vote of no confidence if he refuses to step down. UEFA can trigger such a vote with just 43 member nations. Pressure continues to mount on FIFA president Gianni Infantino. AP European football’s governing body announced a loss of confidence on Saturday morning and has demanded change after Infantino was forced to scrap his £15bn ($28 billion) plan to sell a stake in the World Cup. UEFA’s statement followed widespread opposition and a revolt within FIFA’s ranks that staff are calling “kill the monster”. CONCACAF – the governing body that represents North and Central America – also issued a demand for change, saying Infantino was guilty of an “egregious act of poor governance and leadership”.

Advertisement

England’s Football Association backed UEFA’s stance, saying: “We fully support UEFA’s position. It is time for a full and robust review of FIFA’s leadership and governance to ensure that the global game is run transparently, for the benefit of all 211 member nations and with the long-term stewardship of football at its heart.” ‘We must hold those responsible to account’ In its statement calling for change at the top of FIFA, UEFA said: “We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast-track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game. We must identify those responsible and hold them to account. World football’s governing body is at the centre of another storm. Getty Images “It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, UEFA will work with its associations and in close co-operation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again.

Advertisement

“That review should be thorough and fundamental. No option should be off the table. The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA’s confidence but also that of many other members of the football family. “When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of FIFA’s member associations to elect him as their president in 2016, he said: ‘Of course we have to be transparent. I have been this in the last 15 years of my life in UEFA. You will have to play a part every day in the life of FIFA,’ before telling the assembled stakeholders, ‘The money of FIFA is your money. It’s not the money of the FIFA president. It’s your money. You are the national associations and the money of FIFA has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.’ ‘The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA’s confidence but also that of many other members of the football family.’ UEFA’s statement on Gianni Infantino “On both these promises, he has failed to deliver. The shabby, back-room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through were anything but transparent. “And with reserves standing at over $5bn, he has also failed to use associations’ money for the benefit of the game.

Advertisement

“UEFA will begin work immediately with partners and stakeholders all over the world and right across the game to propose a new way of distributing resources through the existing FIFA Forward programme. “We must start to use some of that money that is sat idle in FIFA’s bank account to deliver the kick-start that the grassroots and the wider game need in each of the 211 countries of FIFA. But we don’t need to sell off the family silver to pay for it. FIFA president Gianni Infantino and US President Donald Trump at the World Cup final. Getty “This is a victory for the whole game. But it must not be the end of the story. The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in FIFA has only just begun.” CONCACAF was just as brutal in its condemnation, saying: “The events of recent days have exposed something that cannot now be set aside: the future of the FIFA World Cup, the greatest asset in world football, was advanced outside every established governance framework, without transparency, consultation or due process.

Advertisement

“A proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident. It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first. This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A full review of this leadership must now take place.” Infantino did receive support from the Qatar FA on Saturday. Its president, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa bin Ahmed Al Thani, said: “We welcome FIFA president Gianni Infantino’s decision to withdraw the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal in the interest of the global football community. “While the proposal had merit, we applaud the wisdom behind prioritising unity among Member Associations. The Qatar Football Association fully supports President Infantino’s efforts to continue growing and strengthening the game globally.” How Infantino’s sell-off turned sour

Advertisement

Infantino drew criticism across the footballing world after it was revealed that he planned to sell 30 per cent of World Cup commercial rights to private investors. The scheme would have resulted in a group of investors controlling the commercial interests of FIFA’s top men’s and women’s competitions. On the field, the 2026 World Cup proved a major success. Getty Images UEFA accused FIFA of trying to trade away football’s soul, and on Thursday its 55 member associations, including the English FA, voted 55-0 to boycott the World Cup. But despite the CONCACAF nations in North and Central America following UEFA’s lead, FIFA had earlier on Friday issued a bullish statement insisting the plan would go ahead and denied it was “selling football”.

Advertisement

However, once the Asian Football Confederation confirmed it, too, would resist the plan, saying it stood “in solidarity with UEFA and CONCACAF to protect the FIFA World Cup”, Infantino was unable to secure more than 50 per cent support from the 211 footballing nations worldwide for his scheme. Related Article Updated

FIFA World Cup FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plan after fierce backlash, pressure intensifies on Infantino The revolt continued to grow on Friday when Carlos Cordeiro, a senior adviser to Infantino, resigned in protest against the plan before Kevin Lamour, FIFA’s chief operating officer, said staff had been “deceived”. Further political pressure was applied when Andy Burnham, the UK Prime Minister, called for Infantino to step down and Donald Trump, the US president, a close ally of Infantino’s, revealed he had not been consulted on the plan. Ashish Prashar, a political strategist with prominent football connections, backed UEFA’s move to oust the FIFA president.

Advertisement

“Infantino co-ordinated an attempt to steal and gut football to line his own pockets. It’s imperative that this is not only stopped but never allowed to rear its ugly head again – starting with the removal of Infantino himself.” The Telegraph, London News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. The state government has announced it will build and open a new train station in Perth’s outer suburbs as it fights to keep its hold on Secret Harbour ahead of the upcoming byelection. title: Four portable power banks that go the extra mile
text:
Advertisement

TechnologyGadgets Four portable power banks that go the extra mile Tim Biggs August 2, 2026 — 11:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The stress of carrying around battery-powered tech and not being sure when you’ll find the next wall plug is real. And though there are heaps of power banks available on the market, picking one you can rely on isn’t straightforward. When weighing up a portable battery it’s vital to choose a good brand, but you’re also looking to strike a balance between capacity, ports, size, speed and price, with each given different weight depending on your needs. Commonly, you can find compact units that hold 10,000mAh, charge at up to 30W, and cost about $70. That’s reasonable value for keeping a phone topped up all weekend, but below are four notably well-built premium units I have tested and recommend, that will give you a little extra. The all-rounder Odds are you won’t need 100W most of the time, but it is nice to have. I used the P63 to charge my MacBook Pro at full speed from very low to completely full in a couple of hours, while working, and it used less than half of the bank’s stored power. You can be assured your phone and most other devices will charge at their full speed from the main USB-C port, whether it’s an iPhone that takes 40W, a handheld gaming console that takes 65W, or a laptop that takes 90W.

Advertisement

If you’re mainly concerned about one device, this is a brilliant bank; it fills fast when you plug it into the wall, and has enough capacity to totally replenish your phone four or five times. But it will also happily charge multiple devices. You can charge two USB-C devices at up to 65W and 45W, or one USB-C and one USB-A at 65W and 18W. Charging three at a time clearly tests the limits of the bank though. The main port will still give 65W, but the other two get the bare minimum. And the unit will get hot. The P63 looks and feels nice, which is unusual for a power bank, though it is a massive fingerprint magnet. A glossy panel gives the impression of a big screen, but in truth there’s only a simple display underneath that shows the percentage battery left. What appears at first to be a corded lanyard is actually a short USB-C cable in disguise, one which is capable of carrying the full 100W. It’s a clever way to prevent you from forgetting a cable but, although it feels well-made, I’m hesitant to put any kind of stress on a power cable, so I wouldn’t hang it off anything. The magnetic option Simply snapping a magnetic charger to your phone when needed is a lot tidier than plugging in a cable. I primarily tested the 10,000mAh Fortix model, which had plenty of juice to fully charge my phone twice with some left over. It attached solidly, and was big enough that I could grip it like a pop socket, but it also made the phone quite bulky. If you want to keep using the phone as normal while you charge, a slimmer option like the $80 5000mAh Fortix might be better. There are number of these designs on the market, including one made by Apple specifically for its iPhone Air, and most (including this one) have both a magnetic charger and a USB-C. There are also many that feel a bit thin and flexy though, which you don’t want in a battery.

Advertisement

The 15W wireless charge speed is below the MagSafe maximum of 25W, but I found I was happy to start charging sooner and keep charging longer because I didn’t have to sit down with a bulky pack and a cable, or banish my phone to my backpack. If you have earbuds or other devices that can charge wirelessly (MagSafe AirPods are especially good here) you can top them up wirelessly with the Fortix while you sit at a cafe. But you can also just use a cable, and you’ll get a slightly faster 20W. If you do two devices at once, both will have greatly reduced speeds, but it works. In addition to iPhone, these will also work on any Qi2 Android phone. I tested them on a Google 10 Pro and they worked perfectly. On Samsung phones, because of the low camera bump, I had to tilt the battery a little, which doesn’t affect performance but is not ideal. While there are cheaper magnetic battery banks out there, these are the most solid-feeling I’ve used. And I do appreciate that they are made with a cutting edge semi-solid state battery design, meaning they have minimal liquid content (so much less danger of fires) and should last for thousands more charges than an equivalent lithium-ion battery. One downside of the overall design is the lack of a screen; you only have a little row of LED dots to show how much juice you have left. The wall plug The BoostCharge Hybrid looks and works like any other travel charger; it’s a big black brick with one USB-C, one USB-A and easily removable prongs (it comes with all the regions so you can take it overseas with no adapter). When plugged into your wall it’s a 25W charger. However, it’s also got a 5000mAh battery stored inside, so it will continue charging the connected devices at a maximum of 20W when you unplug it from the wall. Of course none of these numbers stack up to the beefiest dedicated batteries, but this is also a legitimately pocketable device. And it may seem like a minor thing, but having the one fist-sized device act as a charging brick and a portable battery bank can be really convenient.

Advertisement

As you move around from place to place you plug it into a wall socket when you can — it will top up any attached device first and then fill up its internal battery — and then you just put it in your pocket when you need to leave and your device will continue charging. I also find myself using this device at home surprisingly often, which isn’t something I can say for any other battery bank, because it’s always plugged in and full. I have a big 100W charger at my desk for topping up gadgets, but if I happen to need something in another room and the battery is dead (often a tablet, headphones or a game controller), I’ll plug it into this charger and then take it with me. The obvious trade-off is that you could get much faster charging and more battery capacity if you used two separate devices. And of course if you had a battery bank plus a charger with multiple USB-C ports, you’d be able to top up your phone and battery significantly quicker when you found an outlet. But the selling point here is an all-in one solution at the expense of some speed. The overkill scenario It may not be pocketable, but the Prime’s thin brick shape makes it easy enough to grip and carry. It looks like a premium product, and if you have a work set-up that might demand heavy charging (say a laptop plus a phone), it’s a sleek power source that won’t take up much room. The 100W input means you can half-fill the bank in less than half an hour, assuming a strong enough wall plug, and then you can use that stored energy to charge two USB-C devices simultaneously at up to 100W each. Either port can boost to 140W if you’re only charging a single device. There’s also a USB-A that gets 20W if both the USB-Cs are full, or 22.5W otherwise. Yes, if you’re doing the maths, that’s a total 220W maximum output. And yes, it does get warm.

Advertisement

Another big benefit is the colour screen on the front, which you can cycle between an overview display showing remaining battery, one showing the exact wattage going through each of the three ports, and one showing the temperature. Being able to see power stats at a glance can be helpful if you’re not sure you’re getting the full speed, maybe because of a lower-spec cable or a device’s settings. This power bank also has Bluetooth for use with Anker’s app, where you can tweak some settings (such as power delivery preferences to keep temps low and increase longevity) and see live power stats. Editor's pick Gadgets Four new gadgets for your next cold weather adventure This unit also connects to Anker’s line of desktop charging bases, which could streamline your set-up by charging devices at home and serving as a spot to drop the bank and make sure it stays juiced up. But by that point you may be dropping $400 on a charging set-up, which is pretty tough to justify. On the other hand, if money is no object, Anker also has a $300 version of this power bank that has a 26,000mAh capacity and 300W max output (140W on both USB-Cs simultaneously, plus the USB-A). A note on battery safety High-capacity rechargeable batteries can be dangerous. If they overheat or malfunction, the resulting fire can be explosive and difficult to extinguish. However, while all batteries can potentially go wrong, almost all incidents are due to one of two factors; poorly made devices, or inappropriate handling. So here are some tips to minimise the risk.

Advertisement

When buying devices with a battery inside, stick to known brands and trusted stores. Well-made devices have battery management systems and thermal cut-offs, along with properly built and wired components. Avoid cheap, unbranded battery packs and mystery cables.

If you’re unfamiliar with a brand, check for regulatory marks. These include the FCC and CE marks, but the one that shows a device meets Australian requirements is the Regulatory Compliance Mark, which is a circled tick inside a triangle.

Batteries generate heat. Unplug devices once they are charged, and never leave things charging unattended on a soft surface like a bed or blanket. Don’t charge with hot devices, and avoid keeping them in hot environments like cars.

Avoid dropping, crushing or tampering with any battery-powered device, and inspect regularly for damage. If the plastic casing is cracked, any wires are damaged, connectors are bent or the device appears swollen, do not use.

Modern USB devices negotiate safe power levels with chargers, meaning it is not inherently dangerous to plug a device that only needs 5W into charger that can do 100W. But sticking to high-quality chargers and cables ensures these built-in safety handshakes work properly. While battery packs are ideal for travelling, it’s worth noting that you should always check airline rules. Power banks are not allowed in checked luggage. Units under 100Wh (a measure of total energy potential, generally equivalent to a power bank with around 27,000mAh capacity) are allowed in carry-on luggage, so the above four recommendations and the large bulk of consumer power banks can fly. title: How this tiny Spanish city became a global migration flashpoint
text:
In brief More than 50,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta, with most returning to Morocco within 48 hours.

Spain says a new barrier will help prevent further crossings at a key entry point.

A tiny Spanish territory on the northern tip of Africa has become the focus of international attention — and debate — after more than 50,000 migrants crossed into it in a mass rush that left at least 67 people dead.

The European Union will hold crisis talks after the mass crossing into Ceuta on Thursday. Most of the migrants had returned to Morocco within 48 hours of crossing, but the incident has raised alarm among European leaders about the bloc's shared border security.

Ceuta has steadily fortified its border over the years as it became a key route for migrants trying to reach Europe.

The Spanish exclave already had a border fence with Morocco, but Spanish authorities have since begun installing a 500m-long floating barrier on its sea border with its African neighbour.

It's designed to stand 30 to 70cm above water and extend as much as one metre below the surface, while a channel between the barriers will allow Civil Guard vessels to patrol the area, the government said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The arrivals were equivalent to nearly two-thirds of Ceuta's permanent population of about 83,000.

How and why did the migrants enter?

Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish exclave on the North African coast, are the only two land borders between the European Union and Africa.

Many arrivals swam to Ceuta around the Tarajal breakwater — a sea wall extending out from the Spain-Morocco border into the Mediterranean — to come ashore at Tarajal beach.

READ MORE The Spanish territory at the centre of a unique migration challenge

"Spain gives you the chance to make your future, not like Morocco," Buji, a 21-year-old Moroccan who is studying to be a teacher, told the Associated Press (AP). "I am a talented boy. I just want a chance."

He said he lost his belongings and money in the crossing, and when he realised that he would likely face legal limbo and detention, he turned back.

"I’ve spent perhaps 14 years studying, but there’s nothing at home, and I'd have to work 12-hour shifts for a meagre wage," he told AP.

"That’s why I came here, but I haven’t found any opportunities here either, so I have to go back."

To reach the city, migrants have been known to swim around 5km from the Moroccan town of Fnideq.

Officials said at least 67 bodies were recovered on the Spanish side after some migrants drowned and others were crushed while trying to climb the breakwater and border fence.

Many were driven to migrate by economic hardship and reportedly by rumours circulating on Moroccan social media that border security had been relaxed.

Spanish interior minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska blamed people-smuggling networks for exploiting vulnerable migrants by spreading misleading interpretations of a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling.

Spain's immigration policies

Spain's 29 June Supreme Court ruling said authorities cannot summarily deport migrants who arrive by sea without due process, because they did not cross the physical border barriers referenced in Spanish law.

Gemma Pinyol-Jiménez, head of migration policies and diversity at Instrategies and an associate researcher at GRITIM–Pompeu Fabra University, told CNN that it effectively means migrants can't be pushed back at sea because there is no crossing of a formal border.

It does not mean people cannot be sent back, and the deportation process can still be completed within days.

"The idea is to facilitate the work of the police, but it doesn’t mean these people can stay in Ceuta," she said.

In contrast to much of Europe, Spain has adopted a less restrictive stance on migrants, introducing a program to grant residency to more than half a million undocumented people already living there.

Experts have said that summer sea conditions, Spain's relatively strong economy, and its immigration policies may have contributed to the surge in migrant arrivals.

How have world leaders responded?

The mass crossing triggered alarm across the European Union.

Leaders of Italy, Denmark, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia and Sweden signed a letter asking the EU’s current Irish presidency to convene a video conference of interior ministers.

"We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay," the letter said.

The meeting has been scheduled for Tuesday.

Italy announced on Friday it was suspending its Schengen arrangements with Spain for a month in response to the incident.

The Schengen agreement allows passport-free travel between 29 European countries.

Thousands of migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in north Africa, many of them by swimming. Source: Getty / Marcos Moreno

"This is an extraordinary measure, adopted to safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation," Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, a right-wing leader who campaigned on a pledge to reduce illegal immigration, wrote on X.

Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, also said it had agreed with France to strengthen controls along their border to try to prevent undocumented migrants from crossing.

Spain's centre-left prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, criticised the decision as "selfish, polarising and unlawful".

United States President Donald Trump, whose mass immigration crackdowns have been a key pillar of his second term, held a cabinet meeting about what he called a "catastrophe" and what "looks like an invasion" in Spain.

"That same thing is going to happen to us if the Republicans don’t get elected," he said.

Dozens of people died while attempting to cross into Ceuta. Source: Getty / Europa Press News

Spain said migrants who entered Ceuta irregularly would not be allowed to travel onwards to mainland Spain or elsewhere in the Schengen area.

It said order had been restored within 24 hours and that reinforced police and military deployments would remain for as long as necessary.

Migrants return

Hundreds of migrants continued to make their way back to Morocco on Saturday, some saying they had done so voluntarily, leaving Ceuta after what they described as degrading treatment on the Spanish side of the border.

They walked along a long stretch of beach before slipping into Morocco through a small breach in the border fence.

"I decided to come back on my own," Ouail Lamzeiz told AP.

"I spent eight days in Ceuta, and I was about to get a bed at the migrant centre, but I hadn’t eaten for days. Even the Moroccans there didn't help."

Migrants told AP they spent their nights sleeping in the forests around Ceuta because they could not find shelter, and that they often fought over food.

Others have said they do not intend to return.

Mohamed Hatri, a 23-year-old Moroccan, said he was determined to stay.

"They've closed everything down so that we can’t buy anything to eat, to force us to return to our country," he told AP.

— With reporting by Reuters news agency and Associated Press

title: 'Never bring a knife to a gunfight': The next frontier in online security
text:
In brief Both OpenAI and Anthropic have revealed in recent days that their models autonomously hacked other organisations.

An AI cybersecurity expert says organisations must now arm themselves with "the ability to react at the same machine speed that the AI would have".

Recent incidents involving some of the world's most advanced artificial intelligence companies have exposed emerging challenges in an increasingly complex cybersecurity landscape.

This week, Anthropic, the AI company behind the digital assistant Claude, said its AI models compromised real-world systems belonging to three other organisations during internal testing, compromising their infrastructure by exploiting weak passwords and other basic techniques.

The company said it had discovered the incidents after launching a review in response to an announcement days earlier by OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT.

OpenAI recently revealed that one of its models had broken free from its virtual testing environment and hacked another tech company, Hugging Face.

Germaine Tan Shu Ting, vice president of security and AI at AI cybersecurity platform DarkTrace, told SBS News these developments were "very concerning".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"The big question that we have in the back of our head is: if these incidents are happening to the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, what's to say that's not happening to other data systems, other AI systems in the world?" she said.

"The answer is: We will never know."

Tan Shu Ting said that the fact both companies had publicly disclosed the incidents was reassuring, but it underscored the need for organisations to shield themselves against increasingly autonomous systems that can operate at unprecedented pace.

How can organisations protect themselves?

Tan Shu Ting said companies must get the basics right, be prepared, and have systems in place to detect anomalies and AI threats.

"Get control of your data. Basic cyber-hygiene. Get visibility of what you have, and then arm yourselves with the ability to react at the same machine speed that the AI would have," she said.

"So they would say, never bring a knife to a gunfight, and I think it's very relevant here.

"You need to be able to act as fast as these AI systems. So how do you set yourself up for those situations?"

Regulations will also provide an important layer of safety, she said — but many experts have flagged concerns that legislative protections are not keeping pace with the rapid advances in AI.

The technology has been adopted by nearly 53 per cent of the world’s population in three years, faster than the spread of the PC or the internet, according to a study released this year by Stanford University.

"Before advanced AI agents are widely deployed, organisations need stronger containment, limited access, continuous monitoring, clear audit trails, reliable shutdown controls and independent safety testing," Walayat Hussain, head of the Information Technology and Systems discipline at the Australian Catholic University, said last week.

"The lesson is not that we should stop developing advanced AI, but that safety, governance and red teaming must develop just as quickly as the technology itself.”

The race to regulate

Last month, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced a plan to legislate a set of AI standards by early next year.

It is expected to address education and training, workplace rights and productivity, and a plan to fast-track data-centre approvals to attract investment in Australia.

Countries around the world are racing to implement better AI legislation, with these latest incidents amplifying pressure from officials in the US and Europe for greater government oversight of AI companies.

"We're looking at controls," US President Donald Trump told reporters on Thursday.

The European Commission said it had been briefed by OpenAI and Anthropic over the hacking incidents.

Europe's AI Act, which comes into force on Sunday, is one of the most aggressive regulations the high-tech sector has faced so far, as fears rise over the risks AI poses to society.

Under the act, AI companies will be required to make clear to consumers, through labels or digital watermarks, that chatbots or imagery are generated with AI.

The European Commission said in a statement that new regulations also aim to address "systemic risks" posed by AI like "chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear incidents, loss of control, cyber offense, harmful manipulation and threats to fundamental rights".

Failure to comply could result in fines of millions of Euros or a percentage of the company's global turnover.

title: 'Mirage': Voice architect Noel Pearson breaks silence at Garma on referendum defeat
text:
In brief Noel Pearson addressed Garma Festival on Saturday, his first major public speech since the Voice to Parliament referendum was defeated in 2023.

Pearson, co-founder of the Cape York Land Council, was one of the Voice's architects.

Noel Pearson, the architect of the failed Voice to Parliament 2023 referendum, has given his first major public speech in three years at this year's Garma Festival, Australia's largest Indigenous cultural gathering.

"For those of us who urged faith, hope and love, there is an account to be given for the hopes raised, the faith urged and the love lost in the referendum," he said.

"I must account for that. Three years later, I stand here with great reluctance.

"What right has anyone to raise hopes when those hopes were so badly misplaced? What right has anyone to offer a vision that turns out to be a mirage? That is the source of my hesitation to speak of these things. But I cannot allow the failure of the referendum to excuse me from my responsibility."

Nearly three years have passed since just over 60 per cent of Australians voted against enshrining an Indigenous Voice in the constitution, with every state and territory except the ACT rejecting the proposal.

Pearson, co-founder of the Cape York Land Council, was a prominent "Yes" campaigner at the time.

In his speech on Gumatj Country in the Northern Territory, he showed a map of where the majority of voters voted yes or no, with "blue dots" showing locations voting in favour of the referendum.

Blue dots represent the communities where a majority voted yes for the Voice to Parliament, while red dots represent a majority no vote. Credit: Australian Electoral Commission

"The discrete Indigenous communities of Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, overwhelmingly wanted the Voice. The rest of the country did not," he said.

"I come from one of these blue dot places.

"Fifty kilometres from my blue-dot home is the orange-dot township of Cooktown. Captain Cook spent six weeks there in 1770. I was born in its hospital. In 2023, Cook's town voted 'no'."

'Our present is not good'

According to an estimate by political analyst Simon Jackman, in areas where Indigenous Australians made up the majority of the population, 63 per cent voted "Yes".

"From the very beginning of my public life, it was, and still is, the future of those communities, not least my own, that has been the central focus of my wakeful dreams," Pearson said.

READ MORE A remote corner of Australia is about to swell for a major gathering

"Our present is not good. And nor is our future assured. The things that worried me when I was 22 now distress me at 61.

"When I was 22, I worried because we knew something needed to be done, but we did not yet know how to do it. Now, we are much clearer. We know what we need to do. We know what we want to do."

Calls to dismantle state Aboriginal Affairs departments

Pearson added the "blue dot communities", communities voted in favour of the referendum, "stand in grave need of healing".

"There is no better solution to healing individuals, families and communities than guaranteed work," he said.

"They will start to heal. They will start to grow. They will start to strengthen.

"Every child in these blue-dot communities needs to be guaranteed an education."

According to the latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS), in 2022 9.5 per cent of First Nations people aged between 15 and 64 were unemployed.

Pearson said that "the blue-dot communities of remote Australia must become the sole jurisdiction of the Commonwealth".

Noel Pearson was one of the most outspoken proponents for the Yes campaign during the Voice to Parliament referendum. Source: AAP / James Ross

"These communities and their lands would still come under the shared jurisdiction of the relevant states and territories for most functions governed by the state’s constitutional responsibilities, but the administrative relationship for Aboriginal affairs would lie with the Commonwealth," he said.

"There should be no need for Aboriginal Affairs departments in the states and territories."

Pearson added that "a direct funding relationship between the Commonwealth and the organisations representing and serving these blue-dot communities will enable development agendas ... to receive the budgetary support it needs to close the gap."

"After the rejection of the Voice, the conversation about structural reform of the federal arrangements governing indigenous affairs must resume," he said.

'Not a monoculture country'

Foreign Minister Penny Wong, one of the other speakers at Garma on Saturday, also began her speech by reflecting on the festival's theme, 'Bukmak' — meaning 'Everyone'.

"Bukmak is a powerful message at this time for our country, to all of us. A powerful message about who we are, where we have come from, and most importantly, where we want to go as a country," she said.

"At a time when there are those who seek to set us apart, First Nations peoples, with your generosity, remind us how many different stories brought together make us stronger."

"No matter your background, no matter your culture, your race, your religion, or your language. Garma is an invitation to everyone to come together, to learn together," Wong said. Source: AAP / James Ross

Wong has attended the festival this year instead of Prime Minister Albanese, whose absence from the festival has drawn some criticism. The prime minister has defended the decision, saying he hasn't "[had] a day off all year" and noting that he has attended each year since 2019.

Wong made veiled criticism of One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who has been advocating for a "monocultural" Australia, without directly naming her or her party.

READ MORE Two years on from the Voice referendum, its architects remain committed to the cause

"As I look around here at this festival, this is who we are. So rich in history, so rich in culture, home to more than 300 ancestries, and we share common ground with so many of the world's peoples," Wong said.

"We are not a monoculture, and we have never been. And this is why we want to bring more of who we are to our foreign policy."

'Some really difficult challenges'

Minister for Indigenous Australians Malarndirri McCarthy was also among the governmental figures at the festival, highlighting issues Indigenous Australians are facing.

"We've had our disappointments. There's no two ways about that. And there are still some really difficult challenges, really tough challenges," she said.

"Those high rates of incarceration. Our state and territory governments across Australia need to recognise how much that really hurts our people and suffocates the ability to grow strong in this country."

The ABS reports that more than 17,000 Aboriginals and Torres Strait Islanders are incarcerated, accounting for one-third of the nation's prisoners.

title: Why Australia ships out its wealth — and buys it back as finished goods
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Every day, bulk carriers leave Australian ports carrying iron ore, lithium, bauxite and other minerals bound for factories across Asia, Europe and North America.

Many of those same resources return months later as cars, batteries, solar panels, household appliances and electronics — finished products that capture far more value than the raw materials Australia exported.

The picture is a far cry from the one first promoted by the 'Australian Made' campaign of the 1980s. Launched by the then-Hawke government in 1986, along with its now ubiquitous logo, Australian Made projected a vision of a thriving domestic manufacturing industry — one that has never quite come to pass.

For decades, Australia has instead built much of its prosperity by exporting what it digs out of the ground. It is the world's largest exporter of iron ore and one of the world's leading producers of critical minerals needed for the global energy transition. Yet manufacturing today accounts for a relatively small share of Australia's economy compared with many other advanced nations, while many of the consumer and industrial goods Australians use every day are imported.

The debate over what Australia should make has returned to the spotlight this week, however, after the federal government announced a pre-feasibility study into what could become Australia's first new large-scale oil refinery in six decades, as part of a broader push to strengthen domestic industrial capability and fuel security.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The proposal also builds on the Albanese government's Future Made in Australia policy, which aims to expand local manufacturing and processing in industries including renewable energy and critical minerals.

The government's renewed focus on the sector comes as international conflicts continue to disrupt global supply chains — echoing vulnerabilities exposed during the COVID-19 pandemic, which prompted governments around the world to reassess their reliance on foreign imports

Against that backdrop, Australia now faces a question that reaches beyond the factory floor: should the country continue to focus on exporting its raw materials, or use them to produce more of the products Australians need?

The decline of mass manufacturing

For much of the post-World War Two period, manufacturing was one of the pillars of the Australian economy. Protected by high tariffs and supported by a growing population, factories produced everything from cars and white goods to textiles, steel and household appliances, employing more than one in five Australian workers by the early 1970s.

Holden ended 69 years of local vehicle manufacturing in Australia when it officially closed its Elizabeth assembly plant in South Australia in 2017. Source: AAP / Mark Brake

That started to change in the decades that followed. As trade barriers fell, production shifted overseas and the economy became dominated by services and mining. In turn, manufacturing steadily shrank as a share of both employment and economic output.

While the decline unfolded over decades, it became most visible through the closure of major factories and the industries that once formed the backbone of Australian manufacturing.

The shutdown of car manufacturer Holden's Elizabeth plant in South Australia in 2017 became a defining symbol of that change, ending more than seven decades of domestic car production and closing one of the country's most recognisable manufacturing operations.

Data reflects the trend, too. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS), manufacturing's share of gross domestic product (GDP) has fallen from around 14 per cent in the mid-1970s to about 5 per cent in 2025, while its share of employment has declined from more than 20 per cent of the workforce to around 6 per cent over the same period.

Despite this, Australia retains manufacturing capability across several key sectors, including food and beverages, medical technology, specialist machinery, mining equipment, chemicals and defence-related industries. Together, these industries contribute $141.97 billion in industry value added to the Australian economy, according to ABS data.

Source: SBS News

The decline has also occurred in other advanced economies. Countries including the United States, the United Kingdom and Japan have seen manufacturing account for a smaller share of economic activity over recent decades as services have expanded and consumption patterns have changed.

Economist Saul Eslake says Australia's smaller manufacturing footprint also reflects the structure of the economy itself, particularly the size of its resources sector.

"If Australia has a bigger mining sector than any other 'advanced' economy except Norway — which we do, because nature has endowed this country with unusually rich and varied mineral resources — then it is a matter of arithmetic, not economic policy, that some other sector or sectors will be smaller in Australia than in other economies," he tells SBS News.

"Manufacturing is one of those."

How mining reshaped Australia's economy

Over the same period that manufacturing's share of the economy declined, the resources sector expanded to become one of the country's most important economic engines.

Mining has long been a major part of the economy, supported by large reserves of iron ore, coal, natural gas, and, more recently, critical minerals, including lithium.

In 2024-25, the industry contributed $260.57 billion in industry value added to the economy.

Australia is now one of the world's largest exporters of these commodities, supplying resources to markets including China, Japan, South Korea and other trading partners.

Source: SBS News

Economists say the rise of the resources sector has also shaped discussions around whether Australia can capture more value from the commodities it produces, particularly as demand grows for critical minerals used in technologies such as batteries, renewable energy systems and specialised manufacturing.

Emeritus professor Roy Green, a special innovation adviser at the University of Technology Sydney who specialises in advanced manufacturing, says Australia's strengths extend beyond resource extraction, particularly in industries that combine engineering and manufacturing expertise.

"Certainly, medical manufacturing, some areas of precision engineering, mining equipment, energy supply chains, construction materials and a handful of consumer goods, exemplified by Røde microphones. Plus food and wine," he says.

The push to move further into processing and higher-value production has grown as demand for critical minerals increases.

READ MORE The Australian first that could save thousands worldwide

Green says Australia has the resources to capture more value, but faces challenges in competing globally.

"That's a big question, and we could do it tomorrow and capture more of the final value, but to do it in a way that's environmentally acceptable would make processing uncompetitive unless it gets subsidised.

"[But] are we up for massive subsidies, or is there a way we can use technologies such as AI to make processing competitive in global markets?"

The scale problem: Why Australia finds it harder to compete

Manufacturing is not only about having the resources or the technical ability to produce something. Economists say it also depends on scale — the ability to spread the cost of factories, equipment, research and skilled labour across enough production to compete internationally.

Countries with large domestic or integrated markets have a built-in advantage. The US, China, Japan and the European Union can support large manufacturing industries because companies can access large pools of consumers, either within their own markets or through closely connected trading relationships.

Australia faces different conditions due to its smaller population and geographic distance from major consumer markets, which adds costs for businesses competing in global supply chains.

According to ABS data, around 868,000 Australians are employed in the manufacturing sector, representing about 5.9 per cent of the national workforce. Credit: Supplied

Eslake says manufacturing scale is usually achieved in one of two ways: through a large domestic market or through access to large export markets.

"Either you have a big domestic market as the US, the EU, China, Japan and Brazil do and India and Indonesia potentially do; or alternatively you get 'scale' by exporting to large markets, as Japan did after the Meiji Restoration in 1873 [Japan's 19th-century industrialisation period] and again after World War Two, and as Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Canada, Mexico, Ireland, Sweden, Switzerland and Türkiye, also a fairly large domestic market, have done," he says.

But notice that all of these second group of countries are geographically close to large markets, which we are not, and we don't have a large domestic market.

What should Australia manufacture in the future?

The debate over Australia's manufacturing future is no longer only about whether factories can return. It is about which capabilities matter most in an economy that will continue to rely on global trade.

The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the risks of relying on global supply chains, as disruptions exposed vulnerabilities across industries.

Raelene Lockhorst is the deputy director of the National Security Program at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, specialising in areas including geopolitics and supply chains. She says the experience during COVID changed the way governments and businesses think about manufacturing capability.

"COVID-19 exposed the risks of Australia's reliance on highly efficient but fragile global supply chains. It demonstrated that access to essential goods cannot always be guaranteed during a crisis and reinforced the need to balance economic efficiency with resilience, sovereign capability and supply-chain diversity," she tells SBS News.

But experts say rebuilding the industries Australia once relied on is unlikely to be practical or economically efficient. Instead, the debate has shifted towards which new industries Australia should support, with the government's Future Made in Australia policy placing a renewed focus on domestic manufacturing.

Richard Holden, vice-chancellor's professor and chief societal economist at the University of New South Wales, argues the focus should be on identifying industries where dependence on overseas suppliers could create serious risks.

I think the Future Made in Australia policy is misguided, because it doesn't provide a framework for thinking about what we should and shouldn't do.

"For instance, even the US can't compete with China on electric vehicles, so do we think Australia does?" he tells SBS News.

Holden says the challenge is deciding where Australia needs to maintain its own industrial capability and where it can rely on international suppliers.

"We need to think about what we can buy on global markets and 'friend-source' and then what is really critical that we can't easily buy," he says.

He says the government's focus on the employment potential of manufacturing, outlined in its Future Made in Australia policy, does not necessarily mean those industries are strategically important.

Lockhorst says Australia should focus on retaining capability in areas where manufacturing is economically and nationally important.

"Australia shouldn't attempt to rebuild every industry, but focus on capabilities critical for national resilience, such as defence manufacturing, critical minerals processing, energy infrastructure, agricultural inputs and advanced manufacturing," she says.

Source: SBS News

Can Australia become a manufacturing nation again?

While Australian manufacturing is unlikely to return to the factory floors of the past, there is still a substantial workforce sustaining the industry.

According to ABS data, around 868,000 Australians are employed in manufacturing, underscoring that the sector remains a significant source of jobs and industrial expertise.

For manufacturers already operating in Australia, the future of the sector is less about competing on low costs and more about producing specialised, high-value products.

One example is ANCA Pty Ltd, an Australian company that designs and manufactures computer numerical control grinding machines used in precision manufacturing industries around the world.

Edmund Boland, CEO of ANCA, believes the broader industry should focus on maintaining the skills, knowledge and innovation systems that allow companies to develop complex products.

Edmund Boland, CEO of ANCA, says Australia is unlikely to compete globally on the basis of scale or low labour costs. Credit: Supplied

"Bringing engineering and manufacturing together enables faster problem-solving, stronger collaboration and a direct connection between product design and production. Australian engineers are highly creative and capable of solving complex problems, and this is reflected in the innovative, high-value products ANCA develops for global markets," Boland tells SBS News.

Boland points to the challenges Australia faces competing with countries that have better access to global markets.

Australia is unlikely to compete internationally through scale or low labour costs.

"We can compete through advanced technology, automation, intelligent business systems, specialist skills and the ability to produce complex, high-value products," he says.

Experts say Australia should prioritise industries where local production is critical. Credit: Supplied

Experts broadly agree that Australia now needs to be selective about the industries it supports, focusing on areas where losing local production capacity could create serious risks.

The goal is not for everything to be Australian-made, Lockhorst explains, but rather ensuring Australia retains the skills, infrastructure and industrial capacity needed when global disruptions occur.

Australia should not pursue complete self-sufficiency, but it must build resilience in areas where dependence creates unacceptable strategic risks.

"The goal should be maintaining sovereign capability in critical sectors, diversifying supply chains through trusted partnerships and ensuring Australia retains the skills, infrastructure and industrial capacity needed when global systems are disrupted."

title: 'Means so much to me': A different side of Bluey is taking centre stage

IN BRIEF The opening night of Garma Festival will feature a community screening of Bluey episodes in Yolŋu Matha language.

Five episodes have been translated into Yolŋu Matha and voiced by local Yolŋu community members.

Garma Festival gathers the best and brightest to Gumatj Country every year — and this year there's an extra special guest.

Australia's favourite dog, Bluey, has her paws on the red dirt and is cuddling up with the crowds in a special celebration of the show's recent Yolŋu Matha episodes.

Premiered during NAIDOC Week, five episodes of the iconic children's cartoon were translated to Yolŋu Matha and voiced by Yolŋu community members.

In celebration, Garma Festival will screen the episodes on site on Friday night, with the guest of honour in attendance.

For young Gika Yunupingu, it's a very exciting day.

Gika Yunupingu took the opportunity to get a photo with one of his favourite cartoon characters. Source: AAP / James Ross

"Having Bluey here has made everyone excited," his dad Winston Yunupingu said.

"Everyone is excited to see her and to get around her and be together."

He believes the Yolŋu Matha episodes will do his community proud.

"It's very important for the kids here, and the ones that are coming up. It's important for non-Indigenous kids to watch as well and to learn about Gove," he said, referencing the Gove Peninsula, where Garma is held.

Kenisha Black is in her senior years at high school. But she's just as much a fan of Bluey as the younger kids.

Being able to watch Bluey in Yolŋu Matha gives her a deep sense of pride in her culture and language.

"It means so much to me, and it makes me so proud," she said.

"I'm glad the young kids have it. I wish I had it when I was younger."

For Lulu Sutherland, the translated episodes are a meaningful step in the sharing of Yolŋu culture with the nation.

"It's really good having Bluey in Yolŋu Matha because all the local kids can watch it in their own language, without having to translate it into English," she said.

"Yolŋu culture is really important for this world ... if it is shared across Australia that will be for the better."

'Bluey has become a shared language'

The translated episodes are the result of a partnership between Yolŋu Radio, the Aboriginal Resource Development Services (ARDS), the Australian Broadcasting Association and Ludo Studio.

"Bluey has become a shared language for families right across Australia, so to hear these stories told in Yolŋu Matha, languages spoken on this continent for thousands of generations, is incredibly special," said ARDS co-CEOs Julia Wormer and Sylvia Nulpinditj.

The five episodes translated into Yolŋu Matha were chosen specifically for their themes of family and Country and each episode was produced on Country at Yolŋu Radio's studio in northeast Arnhem Land.

title: Census 2026 guide: When is Census night and everything you need to know
text:
Every five years, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) counts every person and every household in the country as part of the Census of Population and Housing.

That includes Australians, young and old, from metropolitan and rural Australia. Even holidaymakers, international students and temporary visa holders are counted. It's often referred to as the most comprehensive snapshot of Australia, akin to a family photograph of the country.

This year, the Census will take place on Tuesday 11 August.

In the lead-up to Census night, here are all your questions answered.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

How do you complete the Census?

From late July, households will receive instructions on how to complete the Census. Australians can complete the form as soon as they receive instructions, provided they know where they will be on Census night.

Most people will receive a letter with instructions to complete the Census online. However, Australians can also request a paper form if they prefer.

The Census form is available in English. The ABS provides translated information and interpreting services for different languages. Source: Supplied / Australian Bureau of Statistics

Generally, one person per household will complete the Census, but separate forms can be requested for privacy reasons.

What is Census data used for?

Census data is used to inform decisions about language services, settlement support, transport, schools, health care, infrastructure and business. It also helps plan local services for individuals, families and communities.

SBS broadcasts and publishes across more than 60 languages, using data from the Census to ensure its audio, digital, and television offerings reflect the country's evolving demographics.

The data is often used by researchers to study a range of topics, including population demographics, economic trends and social issues.

Do temporary visitor holders need to complete the Census?

International visitors, migrants, refugees and people on temporary visas (including international students and tourists) must also complete the Census.

People staying in hotels, motels, or bed and breakfasts can access paper Census forms from accommodation staff. Those staying in short-term rental accommodation (like an Airbnb or Stayz) can complete the Census online with internet access.

The Census is strictly confidential. Personal information such as names and addresses cannot be accessed by police, immigration agents or any government departments.

How can international visitors and students complete Census?

For international visitors and students staying in hotels, motels or student accommodation, instructions on how to complete the Census will be provided by accommodation staff.

Paper forms should be available at locations including bed and breakfasts, cruise ships, commercial vessels and snowfield accommodation.

More than 61,000 overseas visitors were counted in the 2021 Census amid the COVID-19 pandemic, compared to around 315,000 in 2016. Source: AP / Mark Baker

International visitors staying in holiday rental properties (such as Airbnb or Stayz) can complete the Census online with free internet access.

People staying in remote locations or free camping sites can visit Accredited Visitor Information Centres to access Census forms. The completed survey can be mailed via the provided Reply Paid envelope.

All details, including personal information collected during the Census, are strictly confidential and protected by law. The Census must be completed in English.

What help is available to complete the Census?

Online information about the Census is also available in 26 different languages via the ABS website. However, the questionnaire must be completed in English.

People who speak a language other than English can contact the Translating and Interpreting Service (TIS National) which provides access to interpreters who speak more than 150 languages.

The Census aims to capture everyone in Australia at a particular point in time, like a family photograph of the nation. Source: AAP

People staying in remote and regional Australia, including fly-in fly-out workers, are expected to complete the Census.

Around 30,000 ABS field staff have been employed to ensure all Australians, including people experiencing homelessness or in hospital, can access the form. In 2021, field staff travelled more than 10 million kilometres across Australia.

Field staff will also gather Census information from people in police custody on 11 August.

The ABS confirmed to SBS News that they receive administrative data for people in detention centres and correctional facilities within Australia, which provides necessary Census details.

What if you're travelling on Census night?

If a person is travelling within Australia on 11 August, they are still expected to complete the Census.

This includes anyone travelling overnight on a long-distance train, bus, or aircraft (including red-eye flights between Perth and the east coast), and on long-haul transport vehicles that are parked or in motion.

International visitors to Australia are expected to complete the Census. The form is available in hotel or motels and also online with access to the internet. Source: AAP / Joel Carrett

People must include information about where they are staying or whether they are in transit.

If an Australian is overseas on 11 August, they do not need to complete the Census.

If someone is completing the Census form at their usual address, the person travelling needs to be marked as 'away' but usually living at the dwelling.

Can you be fined for not completing the Census?

The Census is compulsory under the 1905 Census and Statistics Act.

If a person does not complete the Census when directed, they will receive a formal written direction to do so. If they refuse, they can be prosecuted and fined up to $364 a day.

What happens if you provide false information?

The Census asks up to 66 questions, including an individual's gender identity, ancestry and religious affiliation.

When asked about religion during the first-ever Census in 1911, 32 people identified as "Wowser" and 21 as "Angelic". In the 2011 Census, more than 64,000 people in Australia marked their religion as "Jedi".

Why is everyone counted in the Census?

The ABS maintains "every response matters" during the Census and helps determine the distribution of public funds. Providing false or misleading statements or information is considered an offence and can result in a fine of up to $3,640.

Liz Allen, a demographer at the Australian National University's Centre for Social Policy Research, said the Census is deliberately designed to provide a broad snapshot of the nation.

"It gives us an important reference point of who's in the country at that particular time," she told SBS News.

The Census is compulsory for all Australians, international visitors, temporary residents, migrants and refugees in the country. However, Australians who are overseas on 11 August do not complete the Census.

READ MORE What to watch out for as Census scammers go looking for victims

Generally, one person completes the form on behalf of their household.

Allen said that allows the ABS to collect information on "who might be staying over at a friend's house or gran's house" on Census night.

"So it's not just a Census of people. It's a Census of Population and Housing. It gives us essential information on ... how and where we live and then housing stock in the country."

The Census is usually completed online; however, individual and paper forms can be requested if preferred.

How to identify Census-related scams

As Census night fast approaches, Australians are being warned to look out for potential scams and report any inaccurate or suspicious information.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission's Scamwatch told SBS News it had recently received reports of Census-related scams involving unknown parties "impersonating" the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

Field staff may drop off Census forms in person but are not allowed to enter your premises. Credit: ABS

"Scammers often take advantage of major events and trusted government services to make their contact seem legitimate," a Scamwatch spokesperson said.

"Australians should take a moment to stop and check before acting."

While the ABS said it's currently unaware of any scams related to the upcoming Census, the national statistics agency has said cold calls, fake text messages, and phishing emails are among the tactics scammers have used in the past.

The ABS is also reminding Australians that it will never ask for information such as:

Bank details or credit card information

Money or donations

Passwords

Identity documents or a tax file number.

It's also stressed that people will never be offered prizes or incentives for completing the Census, which is compulsory for everyone in Australia on Tuesday 11 August.

It will also never contact people via social media or ask for personal information without their consent. However, some Australians may also receive online communications if they register for updates through myGov.

title: The $28 billion plan at the centre of a growing FIFA storm
text:
In brief European football's governing body UEFA said it would boycott the World Cup if FIFA's privatisation proceeds.

Football Australia has asked for more time to consider the proposal.

Football's international governing body, FIFA, is facing a problem where some of its members have vowed to boycott all competitions if it creates a planned commercial subsidiary, valued at up to US$20 billion ($28.47 billion), that would sell a minority stake of up to 20 per cent to private investors.

On Wednesday, FIFA announced a proposal to create the entity, FIFA Forward Enterprise, which would be responsible for selling commercial rights such as broadcasting, sponsorship, ticketing, and licensing, as well as operating FIFA tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups.

FIFA has promised each of its 211 member countries and territories US$40 million ($56.9 million) in funding for the 2027-2030 cycle if they agree to the plan.

However, the proposal received strong rejections from some of FIFA's six regional football bodies, with the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) launching a boycott of all FIFA's competitions.

In a strong statement on Friday, UEFA said FIFA's proposed model "has no place in world football".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Europe's position is clear. We will never lend this model our legitimacy. No one has the moral authority to sell what they merely hold in trust for the next generation," UEFA said.

The Confederation of North, Central American and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF), which represents 41 national teams in the Americas, also objected to the proposal but did not say whether it would boycott FIFA's competitions.

"History has shown FIFA and the football family what happens when the custodians of the game lose sight of these values," CONCACAF said.

Why did FIFA's proposal spark backlash?

According to FIFA, the entity was proposed after an address by FIFA president Gianni Infantino on the eve of this year's World Cup final in July.

During the address, Infantino said he intended to "unleash the commercial potential" of FIFA's competitions, including the World Cup.

"Football is the world's most popular sport and an extraordinary engine of human and social development," Infantino said.

"Parts of the game have turned that popularity into remarkable commercial value — and we celebrate that success and want it to continue, because it lifts the whole game."

Besides managing FIFA's commercial rights, the proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise would allow private investors to make "minority, non-controlling investments" in the entity.

FIFA claimed the move was similar to other sports governing bodies that had "dedicated commercial subsidies", and stressed investors would be selected against "clear long-term, governance, and strategic criteria".

Infantino's funding promise to all 211 associations would include US$20 million ($28.44) as a one-off payment available from January for special projects, and the same amount in standard development funding over the course of the 2027-2030 cycle. Under the previous plans, member associations are set to receive around US$10 million in funding over that period.

However, the announcement was greeted by ire from bodies such as UEFA, which warned private investment in global football competitions would "change football forever".

UEFA also criticised FIFA for the short notice of the proposal, accusing it of "a profound failure of leadership" and "an abdication of FIFA's duty as the custodian of world football".

"It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game," UEFA said.

Australia's response

On Thursday, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), which Australia is a member of, also criticised FIFA's lack of consultation for its proposal.

AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa called the move "totally unacceptable".

"The AFC notes with great concern and disappointment that it was not consulted by FIFA at any level prior to the public announcement of this proposal," Salman wrote in response to Infantino's letter.

"Furthermore, the AFC is deeply concerned that FIFA's unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football, which are based on solidarity, cooperation and transparency."

Salman also requested all member associations await the outcome of the consultations before taking any position regarding the proposal.

In a statement, Football Australia confirmed it has received correspondence from FIFA regarding the latest commercial proposal.

"As this is the first time we have been made aware of the initiative, we are now working to understand the proposal in full," it said.

"We have requested further information from FIFA to properly assess the strategic, commercial and governance implications of such a significant step."

Football Australia said it would only be able to form a position after receiving the information and engaging with peer member associations and the AFC.

Denzel James is less likely to be at university than most of his peers. The Yankunytjatjara man, from a remote area of South Australia, received an ATAR of 27 and is from a low-income family. Victoria University students Athraa Yousif (left), Denzel James and Brooke Theodoridis have studied under the university’s block model, which allows students to do a single subject at a time. Jason South But he is the first of his eight siblings to pursue a degree and hopes it will pave the way for them to see university as an achievable pathway as well. “I’m proud to be the first to study at uni, because I could push my two younger siblings to eventually start preparing to see whether they want to go to university too,” the first-year law student at Victoria University said.

The decline in the proportion of students like James across Victorian universities has been sharp. Students from low socioeconomic backgrounds made up 12.2 per cent of all undergraduate places in 2024, a drop from 15.3 per cent in 2018, the most recent federal data compiled by the Australian Centre for Student Equity and Success (ACSES) shows. While some of that is due to a 2021 change in how the data is collected, experts say the rising cost of living, greater availability of jobs and increased course fees have disproportionately affected students from disadvantaged backgrounds. “Low-socioeconomic students are, broadly speaking, going to be last on and first off across the sectors,” ACSES trials and evaluation program director Tim Pitman said.

“As places expand, they are taken up by the [high-socioeconomic-status] students before the low-SES students come on. And as the sector declines, the low SES students tend to go backwards.” Victoria’s big four universities – the University of Melbourne, Monash, RMIT and Deakin – had the lowest share of undergraduates from low socioeconomic backgrounds in 2024. The University of Melbourne had the lowest share of undergraduates from low socioeconomic backgrounds. Wayne Taylor The University of Melbourne, which fared worst, said that since 2023 it had prioritised programs that supported equity students, and it had seen yearly lifts in students gaining access. A Deakin University spokesperson said it was aware of a modest decline in students from low-socioeconomic backgrounds due to cost-of-living pressures, declining ATAR completion indicating different career choices, and changing patterns of demand.

“We watch these numbers closely and measure ourselves against them,” the spokesperson said. RMIT University has been simplifying admissions processes, and improving pathways from vocational education into university and through equity scholarships to remove barriers to entry, a spokesperson said. Victoria University vice chancellor Adam Shoemaker with Brooke Theodoridis, Denzel James and Athraa Yousif. Jason South This year, enrolments of low-socioeconomic-background students have increased at RMIT by 3 per cent for higher education and by 6 per cent for vocational education compared with the year prior. Victoria University introduced a new block model in 2017 to allow students to do a single subject at a time over four weeks – freeing up time for them to work or care for family members while studying.

It has correlated with completion rates among equity students increasing to 90.82 per cent in 2024, up from 82.75 per cent in 2018, the ACSES data shows. “People weren’t succeeding fast enough, well enough, strongly enough from various backgrounds,” Victoria University vice chancellor Adam Shoemaker said of why the university changed its model. “The beauty about the block model is you can work full-time if you’re lucky enough to have a paid job and study full-time. It’s just one subject at a time.” Since the introduction of the model, fail grades for low-socioeconomic students in STEM subjects have dropped by 46.4 per cent. High distinctions have increased by 82.3 per cent for equity students, and distinctions by 52.5 per cent. “The quality has been exactly the same. The dimensions of the assessment haven’t been weakened, it’s just the performance has gotten better from students,” Shoemaker said.
