title: ‘Olympic-level singing’: London’s legendary Proms offer low-cost thrills in troubled times
text:
Advertisement

WorldEuropeLondon ‘Olympic-level singing’: London’s legendary Proms offer low-cost thrills in troubled times David Crowe August 2, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: There’s a buzz in the warm evening air as thousands of people stream onto the streets near Hyde Park and talk happily about the concert they’ve just seen at a London landmark. We are outside the Royal Albert Hall a little after 9pm, a few minutes after sunset, and the cloudless sky is cornflower blue. I weave through the crowd to find some choir members who have just finished performing. This is the BBC Proms, one of the world’s great music festivals, and tonight’s concert was just one of 86 that will attract thousands this summer. “When the Proms season comes, life changes; a kind of light comes into your diary,” the BBC’s David Attenborough once said. I can see why his remark is quoted so often: it captures the audience’s sheer enthusiasm for weeks of great music. Last Night of The Proms: A quintessentially British experience. AP Over the past weeks and months, I’ve been spending time on some of the unhappy aspects of British life. I’ve met the marginalised people of Luton, the frustrated voters of Wigan and the angry protesters of London who want to stop migration. It was time to enjoy some of the things that can make London life so wonderful. I’ve just emerged from a concert where the Sydney Philharmonia Choirs joined the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra and its Chorus in a performance of Harmonium by John Adams. This was another Australian coup –the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra performed here last year – reflecting how orchestras and choirs from around the world want to be at the Proms.

Advertisement

By the time the audience sings at the Last Night of the Proms on September 12, this year’s festival will probably have reached an audience of 300,000 in person, in addition to several million viewers online and, on the famed last night, a television audience of 3.7 million. This British tradition is still going strong. Setting for the Proms, London’s landmark Royal Albert Hall. David Levene The first choir member I find is Joel Wilkinson, 24, a music teacher from Sydney. He’s on a high after the performance because he has seen the Proms online but has never made it to England. “To get to be in that room and actually perform is ... a pretty surreal experience,” he says. Teresa Benton, 61, is a software developer who joined the Sydney choir only last year after moving from Melbourne. Raised in Glen Waverley, she sang for 36 years with the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra Chorus and its predecessor, the Melbourne Chorale. “To be in the Royal Albert Hall is just something so special,” she tells me. It took months of preparation and practice. Sisters Emily and Lily Harris say the work was intense. “We had about a month of rehearsals before the flight over, and quite intensive rehearsals,” says Emily, a student at the Sydney Conservatorium of Music. In Birmingham, before they got to the Proms, they rehearsed once or twice daily. “It was a lot – almost six hours sometimes,” says Lily, a digital video director.

Advertisement

Will they get to enjoy London in summer? Not much. The choir has more performances coming up, so there is little time to relax. “I think we’ve got two brunches,” jokes Lily. But the sisters can claim a rare family achievement: their grandmother, Sue, sang at the Proms as a member of the Sydney Philharmonia Choirs; their father, Mark, performed there with the Australian Youth Orchestra. Who else in Australia can claim three generations at the Proms? Related Article Analysis

Immigration How the storming of Ceuta shifts Europe to the right As athletes are representing Australia at the Commonwealth Games, it seems appropriate for musicians to be doing the same at the Proms. Brett Weymark, the artistic director of the Sydney Philharmonia Choirs, says it’s a fair comparison because the music festival attracts performers from around the world. “It’s incredibly special that we’re here this time because it has been the better part of 16 years since we were last here,” he says. And he calls the work tonight, Harmonium, one of the most exacting pieces a chorus can perform. “This is Olympic-level choral singing,” he says. “What the athletes are doing in Glasgow, we’re doing here.” Political life in Britain is riven with anxiety about the nation’s economic and social problems, and it is not hard to see the divide between rich and poor. Life in London is easy for those with a club in St James’s and a house in the country, but it can be crushingly hard for the working poor who get by on a minimum wage of £12.71 per hour. (That’s about $24, which is $2 less than the Australian minimum wage.) Going out can be a luxury.

Advertisement

It does not have to be too expensive at the Proms, however. Every morning, people can buy £8 tickets online for the arena and gallery at the Royal Albert Hall. This is standing room only for the “Prommers” – the dedicated audience members who stamp their feet when happy and yell out “Heave” and “Ho” whenever a piano is wheeled on stage. More of that British tradition. Related Article Entertainment Why video game music is the future of orchestral concerts Call me old-fashioned, or simply lazy, but I chose a comfortable seat instead, and I got even more comfortable after a G&T. The Prommers, in their shorts and joggers, or their summer frocks, seemed to be having more fun than the couple in the royal box. (No, not members of the royal family – just people with connections.) Even in these hard times, then, it is still possible to enjoy something that is quintessentially British, on a beautiful summer night, for the cost of a bus fare and an £8 ticket. You can’t see a Premier League match for that, nor a day of Test cricket at Lord’s. No wonder everyone sings Land of Hope and Glory on the last night of the Proms. Edwards aggravated an old shoulder injury making a try-saving tackle on Brisbane’s Josiah Karapani on July 16. The fullback did not feature the following week against Parramatta, with most fans assuming at the time it was to do with the 10 stitches he required for a nasty head gash. Mitch Kenny is yet to return after being injured while playing against the Dolphins. Getty Images Cleary later confirmed it was his shoulder, and while Edwards missed Saturday’s 42-18 win over Canberra, the coach was “hopeful” he would be back for the Warriors game. Before giving him the green light to return, Penrith medical staff are eager to see Edwards complete a range of tackling and contact drills, and want his shoulder to be “at least 90 per cent strength”.

Edwards underwent a Latarjet procedure just days after helping Australia win the Pacific Championships final against Tonga at the end of 2024. He also had a full shoulder reconstruction after he broke down in the early rounds of the 2018 season. Even if Edwards misses the trip to Auckland to face the Warriors, the club expects him back on deck the following week to play the Sydney Roosters. title: Resign or we’ll vote to oust you: Europe’s threat to Infantino
text:
Advertisement

SportSoccerFIFA World Cup Resign or we’ll vote to oust you: Europe’s threat to Infantino Tom Morgan August 2, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Gianni Infantino is facing an ultimatum from European football’s governing body UEFA: resign or face an emergency no-confidence vote. It is understood all 55 of UEFA’s member nations would opt to oust Infantino in a vote of no confidence if he refuses to step down. UEFA can trigger such a vote with just 43 member nations. Pressure continues to mount on FIFA president Gianni Infantino. AP European football’s governing body announced a loss of confidence on Saturday morning and has demanded change after Infantino was forced to scrap his £15bn ($28 billion) plan to sell a stake in the World Cup. UEFA’s statement followed widespread opposition and a revolt within FIFA’s ranks that staff are calling “kill the monster”. CONCACAF – the governing body that represents North and Central America – also issued a demand for change, saying Infantino was guilty of an “egregious act of poor governance and leadership”.

Advertisement

England’s Football Association backed UEFA’s stance, saying: “We fully support UEFA’s position. It is time for a full and robust review of FIFA’s leadership and governance to ensure that the global game is run transparently, for the benefit of all 211 member nations and with the long-term stewardship of football at its heart.” ‘We must hold those responsible to account’ In its statement calling for change at the top of FIFA, UEFA said: “We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast-track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game. We must identify those responsible and hold them to account. World football’s governing body is at the centre of another storm. Getty Images “It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, UEFA will work with its associations and in close co-operation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again.

Advertisement

“That review should be thorough and fundamental. No option should be off the table. The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA’s confidence but also that of many other members of the football family. “When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of FIFA’s member associations to elect him as their president in 2016, he said: ‘Of course we have to be transparent. I have been this in the last 15 years of my life in UEFA. You will have to play a part every day in the life of FIFA,’ before telling the assembled stakeholders, ‘The money of FIFA is your money. It’s not the money of the FIFA president. It’s your money. You are the national associations and the money of FIFA has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.’ ‘The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA’s confidence but also that of many other members of the football family.’ UEFA’s statement on Gianni Infantino “On both these promises, he has failed to deliver. The shabby, back-room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through were anything but transparent. “And with reserves standing at over $5bn, he has also failed to use associations’ money for the benefit of the game.

Advertisement

“UEFA will begin work immediately with partners and stakeholders all over the world and right across the game to propose a new way of distributing resources through the existing FIFA Forward programme. “We must start to use some of that money that is sat idle in FIFA’s bank account to deliver the kick-start that the grassroots and the wider game need in each of the 211 countries of FIFA. But we don’t need to sell off the family silver to pay for it. FIFA president Gianni Infantino and US President Donald Trump at the World Cup final. Getty “This is a victory for the whole game. But it must not be the end of the story. The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in FIFA has only just begun.” CONCACAF was just as brutal in its condemnation, saying: “The events of recent days have exposed something that cannot now be set aside: the future of the FIFA World Cup, the greatest asset in world football, was advanced outside every established governance framework, without transparency, consultation or due process.

Advertisement

“A proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident. It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first. This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A full review of this leadership must now take place.” Infantino did receive support from the Qatar FA on Saturday. Its president, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa bin Ahmed Al Thani, said: “We welcome FIFA president Gianni Infantino’s decision to withdraw the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal in the interest of the global football community. “While the proposal had merit, we applaud the wisdom behind prioritising unity among Member Associations. The Qatar Football Association fully supports President Infantino’s efforts to continue growing and strengthening the game globally.” How Infantino’s sell-off turned sour

Advertisement

Infantino drew criticism across the footballing world after it was revealed that he planned to sell 30 per cent of World Cup commercial rights to private investors. The scheme would have resulted in a group of investors controlling the commercial interests of FIFA’s top men’s and women’s competitions. On the field, the 2026 World Cup proved a major success. Getty Images UEFA accused FIFA of trying to trade away football’s soul, and on Thursday its 55 member associations, including the English FA, voted 55-0 to boycott the World Cup. But despite the CONCACAF nations in North and Central America following UEFA’s lead, FIFA had earlier on Friday issued a bullish statement insisting the plan would go ahead and denied it was “selling football”.

Advertisement

However, once the Asian Football Confederation confirmed it, too, would resist the plan, saying it stood “in solidarity with UEFA and CONCACAF to protect the FIFA World Cup”, Infantino was unable to secure more than 50 per cent support from the 211 footballing nations worldwide for his scheme. Related Article Updated

FIFA World Cup FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plan after fierce backlash, pressure intensifies on Infantino The revolt continued to grow on Friday when Carlos Cordeiro, a senior adviser to Infantino, resigned in protest against the plan before Kevin Lamour, FIFA’s chief operating officer, said staff had been “deceived”. Further political pressure was applied when Andy Burnham, the UK Prime Minister, called for Infantino to step down and Donald Trump, the US president, a close ally of Infantino’s, revealed he had not been consulted on the plan. Ashish Prashar, a political strategist with prominent football connections, backed UEFA’s move to oust the FIFA president.

Advertisement

“Infantino co-ordinated an attempt to steal and gut football to line his own pockets. It’s imperative that this is not only stopped but never allowed to rear its ugly head again – starting with the removal of Infantino himself.” The Telegraph, London News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. title: WA Labor and Liberals battle it out over Karnup train station promise

NationalWAPublic transport WA Labor and Liberals battle it out over Karnup train station promise Hannah Murphy August 2, 2026 — 12:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The state government has announced it will build and open a new train station in Perth’s outer suburbs as it fights to keep its hold on Secret Harbour ahead of the upcoming byelection. Premier Roger Cook announced the $156 million train station for Karnup on Sunday, with Transport Minister Rita Saffioti confirming she would be allocating $10 million to begin planning the station. Mock ups of the Karnup Station posted on the Building for Tomorrow website. Building for Tomorrow Karnup is in the Secret Harbour electorate, which used to be held by WA Defence Minister Paul Papalia before he announced his retirement last month. Running in his place is Labor candidate Georgia Tree, who previously came under fire for living outside of the electorate. She has since moved in with family to stay inside her voter base. Karnup train station was first flagged for the Mandurah Line back in 2013, and has faced extensive delays since.

Advertisement

Related Article Metronet ‘We like to win’: Saffioti and Hastie go head-to-head over Lakelands station Cook said on Sunday population growth in the southern suburb meant the Karnup train station was now top of their agenda. “As part of our long-term Metronet vision, we have always planned for a train station here at Karnup, and today we can announce work will start on the Karnup train station project in 2028,” he said. Cook said WA’s share of the project would be funded by land sales, while they would seek the other half from the federal government. Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said the train station was “always part of the plan”, but accepted the project had been sped up by the upcoming byelection.

Advertisement

“In relation to the timing, look, we would probably have made this announcement over the next six to eight months, but of course we have bought that announcement early,” she said. “Because we have got so much certainty now with the planning ... it’s all coming together.” An artist impression of a proposed new Karnup development, which is expected to bring thousands of new residents to the suburb south of Perth requiring access to rail. Saffioti said the project had been initially held up due to zoning laws and funding issues, due to the prioritisation of the nearby Lakelands train station. Ultimately, Saffioti said the station would be an “elevated design” with more than 400 car parking pays and an eight bus interchange.

Advertisement

Tree said it was clear her government had listened to locals. Warnbro local Georgia Tree has been announced as WA Labor’s candidate for the looming Secret Harbour byelection. 9News Perth “I’ve been talking to thousands of residents in Karnup and surrounding suburbs over the past few weeks,” she said. “I’ve heard loud and clear from my community that they want to see Metronet Karnup Station built – and that’s what I’ve been fighting for and feeding back to the Premier and Deputy Premier at every opportunity. “This is a huge moment for our community with money on the table and works to begin in 2028.”

Advertisement

Related Article WA election Secret Harbour byelection heating up as One Nation announces candidate The Labor government’s announcement comes just five days after opposition leader Basil Zempilas said he would be looking to revive the project if elected. “Labor promised Karnup Station in 2013, again in 2017 and again in 2021. Nearly a decade after Labor came to government, there is still no money in the State Budget, no construction timetable and no delivery date,” he said. “Locals have waited long enough. They deserve a firm commitment, not another promise designed to get Labor through an election.” Zempilas said the Liberals would commit $90 million to the project and commence building in 2029, and Saffioti slammed the figure as “undercosting”.

Advertisement

“There’s no way they’ll deliver it for $90 million,” she said. “Look, they said they’ll deliver an Ellenbrook rail line in 2008, and they never did. They said they’ll deliver max light rail. They came out with a under-costed ‘back of the envelope’ commitment.” Liberal local candidate Ryan Robertson offered his own support for the project, but said only his party had listened to residents about what they wanted from the train station. City of Rockingham councillor Ryan Robertson is WA Liberal’s candidate for Secret Harbour. Facebook/Ryan Robertson “People in Secret Harbour and surrounding suburbs are tired of being told Karnup station is coming,” Mr Robertson said.

Advertisement

“They have watched Labor make the same promise election after election while the station has remained unfunded and undelivered. “Karnup station is essential infrastructure for the future of this fast-growing community.”

title: Four portable power banks that go the extra mile
text:
Advertisement

TechnologyGadgets Four portable power banks that go the extra mile Tim Biggs August 2, 2026 — 11:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The stress of carrying around battery-powered tech and not being sure when you’ll find the next wall plug is real. And though there are heaps of power banks available on the market, picking one you can rely on isn’t straightforward. When weighing up a portable battery it’s vital to choose a good brand, but you’re also looking to strike a balance between capacity, ports, size, speed and price, with each given different weight depending on your needs. Commonly, you can find compact units that hold 10,000mAh, charge at up to 30W, and cost about $70. That’s reasonable value for keeping a phone topped up all weekend, but below are four notably well-built premium units I have tested and recommend, that will give you a little extra. The all-rounder Odds are you won’t need 100W most of the time, but it is nice to have. I used the P63 to charge my MacBook Pro at full speed from very low to completely full in a couple of hours, while working, and it used less than half of the bank’s stored power. You can be assured your phone and most other devices will charge at their full speed from the main USB-C port, whether it’s an iPhone that takes 40W, a handheld gaming console that takes 65W, or a laptop that takes 90W.

Advertisement

If you’re mainly concerned about one device, this is a brilliant bank; it fills fast when you plug it into the wall, and has enough capacity to totally replenish your phone four or five times. But it will also happily charge multiple devices. You can charge two USB-C devices at up to 65W and 45W, or one USB-C and one USB-A at 65W and 18W. Charging three at a time clearly tests the limits of the bank though. The main port will still give 65W, but the other two get the bare minimum. And the unit will get hot. The P63 looks and feels nice, which is unusual for a power bank, though it is a massive fingerprint magnet. A glossy panel gives the impression of a big screen, but in truth there’s only a simple display underneath that shows the percentage battery left. What appears at first to be a corded lanyard is actually a short USB-C cable in disguise, one which is capable of carrying the full 100W. It’s a clever way to prevent you from forgetting a cable but, although it feels well-made, I’m hesitant to put any kind of stress on a power cable, so I wouldn’t hang it off anything. The magnetic option Simply snapping a magnetic charger to your phone when needed is a lot tidier than plugging in a cable. I primarily tested the 10,000mAh Fortix model, which had plenty of juice to fully charge my phone twice with some left over. It attached solidly, and was big enough that I could grip it like a pop socket, but it also made the phone quite bulky. If you want to keep using the phone as normal while you charge, a slimmer option like the $80 5000mAh Fortix might be better. There are number of these designs on the market, including one made by Apple specifically for its iPhone Air, and most (including this one) have both a magnetic charger and a USB-C. There are also many that feel a bit thin and flexy though, which you don’t want in a battery.

Advertisement

The 15W wireless charge speed is below the MagSafe maximum of 25W, but I found I was happy to start charging sooner and keep charging longer because I didn’t have to sit down with a bulky pack and a cable, or banish my phone to my backpack. If you have earbuds or other devices that can charge wirelessly (MagSafe AirPods are especially good here) you can top them up wirelessly with the Fortix while you sit at a cafe. But you can also just use a cable, and you’ll get a slightly faster 20W. If you do two devices at once, both will have greatly reduced speeds, but it works. In addition to iPhone, these will also work on any Qi2 Android phone. I tested them on a Google 10 Pro and they worked perfectly. On Samsung phones, because of the low camera bump, I had to tilt the battery a little, which doesn’t affect performance but is not ideal. While there are cheaper magnetic battery banks out there, these are the most solid-feeling I’ve used. And I do appreciate that they are made with a cutting edge semi-solid state battery design, meaning they have minimal liquid content (so much less danger of fires) and should last for thousands more charges than an equivalent lithium-ion battery. One downside of the overall design is the lack of a screen; you only have a little row of LED dots to show how much juice you have left. The wall plug The BoostCharge Hybrid looks and works like any other travel charger; it’s a big black brick with one USB-C, one USB-A and easily removable prongs (it comes with all the regions so you can take it overseas with no adapter). When plugged into your wall it’s a 25W charger. However, it’s also got a 5000mAh battery stored inside, so it will continue charging the connected devices at a maximum of 20W when you unplug it from the wall. Of course none of these numbers stack up to the beefiest dedicated batteries, but this is also a legitimately pocketable device. And it may seem like a minor thing, but having the one fist-sized device act as a charging brick and a portable battery bank can be really convenient.

Advertisement

As you move around from place to place you plug it into a wall socket when you can — it will top up any attached device first and then fill up its internal battery — and then you just put it in your pocket when you need to leave and your device will continue charging. I also find myself using this device at home surprisingly often, which isn’t something I can say for any other battery bank, because it’s always plugged in and full. I have a big 100W charger at my desk for topping up gadgets, but if I happen to need something in another room and the battery is dead (often a tablet, headphones or a game controller), I’ll plug it into this charger and then take it with me. The obvious trade-off is that you could get much faster charging and more battery capacity if you used two separate devices. And of course if you had a battery bank plus a charger with multiple USB-C ports, you’d be able to top up your phone and battery significantly quicker when you found an outlet. But the selling point here is an all-in one solution at the expense of some speed. The overkill scenario It may not be pocketable, but the Prime’s thin brick shape makes it easy enough to grip and carry. It looks like a premium product, and if you have a work set-up that might demand heavy charging (say a laptop plus a phone), it’s a sleek power source that won’t take up much room. The 100W input means you can half-fill the bank in less than half an hour, assuming a strong enough wall plug, and then you can use that stored energy to charge two USB-C devices simultaneously at up to 100W each. Either port can boost to 140W if you’re only charging a single device. There’s also a USB-A that gets 20W if both the USB-Cs are full, or 22.5W otherwise. Yes, if you’re doing the maths, that’s a total 220W maximum output. And yes, it does get warm.

Advertisement

Another big benefit is the colour screen on the front, which you can cycle between an overview display showing remaining battery, one showing the exact wattage going through each of the three ports, and one showing the temperature. Being able to see power stats at a glance can be helpful if you’re not sure you’re getting the full speed, maybe because of a lower-spec cable or a device’s settings. This power bank also has Bluetooth for use with Anker’s app, where you can tweak some settings (such as power delivery preferences to keep temps low and increase longevity) and see live power stats. Editor's pick Gadgets Four new gadgets for your next cold weather adventure This unit also connects to Anker’s line of desktop charging bases, which could streamline your set-up by charging devices at home and serving as a spot to drop the bank and make sure it stays juiced up. But by that point you may be dropping $400 on a charging set-up, which is pretty tough to justify. On the other hand, if money is no object, Anker also has a $300 version of this power bank that has a 26,000mAh capacity and 300W max output (140W on both USB-Cs simultaneously, plus the USB-A). A note on battery safety High-capacity rechargeable batteries can be dangerous. If they overheat or malfunction, the resulting fire can be explosive and difficult to extinguish. However, while all batteries can potentially go wrong, almost all incidents are due to one of two factors; poorly made devices, or inappropriate handling. So here are some tips to minimise the risk.

Advertisement

When buying devices with a battery inside, stick to known brands and trusted stores. Well-made devices have battery management systems and thermal cut-offs, along with properly built and wired components. Avoid cheap, unbranded battery packs and mystery cables.

If you’re unfamiliar with a brand, check for regulatory marks. These include the FCC and CE marks, but the one that shows a device meets Australian requirements is the Regulatory Compliance Mark, which is a circled tick inside a triangle.

Batteries generate heat. Unplug devices once they are charged, and never leave things charging unattended on a soft surface like a bed or blanket. Don’t charge with hot devices, and avoid keeping them in hot environments like cars.

Avoid dropping, crushing or tampering with any battery-powered device, and inspect regularly for damage. If the plastic casing is cracked, any wires are damaged, connectors are bent or the device appears swollen, do not use.

Modern USB devices negotiate safe power levels with chargers, meaning it is not inherently dangerous to plug a device that only needs 5W into charger that can do 100W. But sticking to high-quality chargers and cables ensures these built-in safety handshakes work properly. While battery packs are ideal for travelling, it’s worth noting that you should always check airline rules. Power banks are not allowed in checked luggage. Units under 100Wh (a measure of total energy potential, generally equivalent to a power bank with around 27,000mAh capacity) are allowed in carry-on luggage, so the above four recommendations and the large bulk of consumer power banks can fly. But the actual use or charging of power banks on planes is now largely prohibited. Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter every Friday. Sign up here.

title: FIFO worker relocates 8,000km to get paid twice as much: 'More possibilities'
text:
FIFO work is widely known to be gruelling due to its long shifts, exhausting routines, and the isolation from loved ones.

However, Japanese expat Ryota Sato has managed to keep a smile on his face despite the mundane routines by dancing and creating fun videos that have made him an online sensation.

Ryota has lived in Australia for about four years, and told Yahoo News it's been enough time for him to realise he doesn't want to go back to Japan.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I used to live in Tokyo for a few years, and then it really cracked me," he said.

While he values the importance of working hard and continues to do so, Ryota said the work environment in Japan was not a "match" for him.

Compared to life in Perth now, the 29-year-old said, "I can feel peaceful" and get paid twice as much.

Lucrative six-figure jobs worth the cost?

While he is "not energetic every day," Ryota says dancing, listening to music, exercising and talking to his friends are just a few ways he has fun at work. Source: Ryota Sato

For many Australians, FIFO's high salaries come at a cost, with some questioning whether the financial gain is worth the struggle.

Ryota, however, says "FIFO is worth it" because of the career experience and financial stability.

He said he values working at a mine site in the Pilbara, collecting and analysing water samples.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

It's not only helped him improve his English, "but also my adaptability, and confidence at work", he said.

"Sometimes it is difficult to communicate with people who have a very strong accent, but I want to push myself and go beyond my comfort zone," Ryota said.

RELATED:

He admits he is not energetic every day, as he has to wake up to 5am alarms to repeat a workday that looks eerily like the last.

"After a long day, I return to camp, eat dinner, and often feel too exhausted to do anything except sleep.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"Then I see the same surroundings, and I follow almost the same routine every day. There isn't much stimulation outside work."

So Ryota said he relies on the "small things" like music, dancing, exercising, talking to his friends, or even "seeing a beautiful sunrise or view."

"I also try to remind myself that even when something feels difficult or inconvenient, like pushing through it, it might lead to something positive in the future," he said.

Turning ordinary, repetitive days extraordinary

Videos of Ryota dancing and documenting his life have been seen by tens of thousands who applauded his vibrant attitude. Source: Ryota Sato

Online, Ryota is seen beaming from ear to ear in videos he shares of his life in the outback.

Watching him dance, smile, and energetically document his life has been well received by thousands, who are delighted to see him so lively.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

While many see Ryota as vibrant and lively, he said he makes fun content as a creative outlet to turn an "ordinary or repetitive workday into something fun."

Ryota said the friendliness of Australians, nature, and diversity are all part of why he will be lodging a permanent residency visa in the new year.

Australia, is the second most popular destination for Japanese citizens living overseas, after the United States and ahead of China, according to the Australian National University.

About 105,500 Japanese nationals live in Australia.

Ryota arrived in Australia in 2022. He's since completed his master's degree in environmental management, travelled the country and started a career in Perth. Source: Ryota Sato

Ryota said that by loudly continuing to be himself, he encourages others to be able to build a career without sacrificing their spark.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"There's a much bigger world and many more possibilities out there than people may currently realise," he said.

"I hope my funny journey, encourages others to take a chance, step outside their comfort zone and discover what might be possible for them."
